I noticed that as well. The dialogue has slowly shifted into being more, for the lack of personal vocabulary, "shipping" focused. There's a lot more talk between the characters of why they love Akira, why Akira should be with them, how the girls view their relationship with Akira, so far and so forth. It's definitely not my favorite dialogue since I enjoy the story as more than just: "Who do I want to see Akira(and by extension, I, the player) get with." I genuinely think the story sits with among the best out there.

There are a few reasons as to why from what I can tell. First, this is the 4th chapter. It'd be weird if the characters were still unaware of Akira's, once again for the lack of better vocabulary, whoring and didn't actively try and pursue his affection. It just makes sense that there is more dialogue revolving around his relationships with the characters this far in.

Also, considering the fact that this game is at the end of the day a porn game, and there are still a handful of characters who haven't even had a sex scene yet, I suspect that Selebus is trying to rush along character arcs to give people who stan certain characters their desired outcome. On some characters it works well like Yumi. Honestly, its nice watching her warm up to Akira, and sense she's aware of the timeloops it takes away the whole, "She's still a minor mentally" thing that every other character still has so I feel little guilt seeing them bond. On other's(Miku) it kind of feels forced. Like, it makes sense that she would be vying for Akira's affection and wanting to have proper physical intimacy, but there's certain dialogue that she says that just makes me see Selebus's hand, which is not something an author should aspire toward.

posts.content_html_raw:
Hey guys. Ignore this post. It's just...

I've been in a weird place for the last half a year and stumbled on this VN two months ago. I am at "How to Fuck Your Father," in the 4th chapter. So...

I usually don't like to theorize while experiencing any kind of media; I prefer to consume it first and analyze later, so I am pretty bad at theories. But I often have hunches on the ways a story can go; I just prefer not to examine them.
But this time... This VN is just too big to keep it on a leash, and since it's hard to go out there expecting people to know about it or discuss it in public, I kinda have to just not think about it. And I usually dont. Not this time, tho. It's throbbing in my brain, wiggling and trying to get out, and I just can't keep it in. To the point where I had to drop the event in the middle of it to come here instead.
I suspect this thread has about 3k of more complex, coherent, and interesting theories, and I am not trying to sound smart; I just... I started "How to Fuck Your Father" and suddenly realized that Ami is just Akira's guardian - subperson he developed to protect himself from childhood abuse. I can only suspect that Sekai wasn't the first one or only one to actually abuse him. I suspect it was either his late brother Nozomu, thus the first God god to ever appear in VN, the creator of Ami, or maybe his literal father (Yuu?.. I may misunderstand this part) thus, Ami always wants to... fuck her father.
The way everyone around Ami who really loves Akira also loves Ami is kinda big factor in this too. Up to this point I was struggling to understand why Niki, Noriko and Akira himself were so loyal to Ami. Like to the point where Niki sees through all the bullshit Ami says to her and insists on loving her.

I thought before that Ami can't be "not real" in this world since we have a lot of scenes with her separately from Akira when something happened to both of them. But... with how fucked up reality in this VN is, it's kinda easy to explain it if you really want to.

But now I try to read "How to Fuck Your Father" without this theory, and I can't. I keep seeing Nodoka provoking Akira to play both Sensei and Ami at the same time to know more about his dissociation, and I just want to experience this scene the old-fashioned way, with my dick in my hand and not in my brains...

It is plausible that right after I post this I will find a sentence in the next few lines of the event that will debunk this theory. For now, though...
I don't want to imagine Akira fucking himself while wearing girl's clothes and talking about his A cups. I am a weirdo, though, so I will tolerate it if I have to. Damn you, Selebus.
Please send help.

posts.content_html_raw:
Welp, since I’m nothing if not dedicated to spending every waking moment of my life thinking about this unholy piece of fiction (to the point where I now get actual withdrawal symptoms from taking even a few days off from LiL), here it is – the thing that I mentioned I was working on about a week ago: an extensive (and at least somewhat comprehensive) list of all/most of the currently unresolved mysteries and plot threads that were directly brought back into relevancy over the course of the last ten updates – starting from the version 0.47 – presented (mostly) in a chronological order of their re-introduction into the spotlight.

Additionally, for the sake of actually talking about something different for once, I deliberately excluded all of the aforementioned mysteries and plot threads that are explicitly related to Ami, Maya, Himawari, Sekai (with a relatively small exception near the very end of the post) or the general workings of the Wishing Well, since I feel like these topics have already been mostly discussed to death by many people here – including me! – and I don’t want to just endlessly reiterate the same two or three talking points.

(PS: I once again had to split this post into two parts – with the second one coming out sometime later this week, whenever I feel like posting it – because I eventually realized that *literally no one* is going to read the whole 10000+ words at once, not to mention actually *process* them in full, so it would be better for me to separate them at least in half so as to not completely overwhelm people here. This way everyone who braves this wall of text will be able to properly sit on my proposed ideas for a couple of days, potentially coming up with their own additions and/or rebuttals to this analysis, which is more beneficial for the sake of having a constructive discussion.)

The first item on our list is the mystery of the second floor of Tojo Ramen: the strange pure-white room that Akira unexpectedly stumbles upon in “WORMGOD54” – a room that contains only a single unassuming metal door, presumably leading directly to Tenchou (implied via both WORMGOD’s narration about how “the door needs to be protected” and Tsuneyo’s later photo-guide of her room in “Defilement of a Temple”, where she says that “my father is the room right beside mine”), as well as a reference to the Upside-Down House (and/or the “there is something buried beneath our feet” line, but that is a subject for a later section) in the form of the cryptic wall graffiti.

Now, despite the fact that we’ve only actually seen this room as late as version 0.47, and the event that introduces it only raises multiple new questions without providing answers to any of the old ones, what some people might not be aware of is that the existence of this location was actually revealed to us all the way back in the very-very beginning of Chapter 3 – version 0.25pt2, to be exact – and it has been referenced *at least* three times even prior to its direct appearance in “WORMGOD54” by multiple meta-aware characters:

The very first mention of the so-called “white room” (presuming that I haven’t missed anything) happens in Yasu’s “Down The Rabbit Hole”, where she initially chastises Penemue for “barely touching his eggs”, since that means that he “won’t be able to come to the white room with us”, and then later – while experiencing what appears to be either a mental breakdown or a possession by some entity (likely HOPE) – begs Sensei to also “partake in their feast that transcends time itself” by eating one of Penemue eggs and thus “reserve your space in the white room”, because “there is nowhere else that can protect us from…” something, though the girl is unable to finish her sentence due to an especially severe bout of headache. The event then concludes with the entire tea party seemingly being completely retconned from existence (*or* an implication that it all took place in Akira’s head, explaining why everyone suddenly “disappeared” and why Yasu recounts a completely different version of these events in her “Sore Thumb”) and Sensei going back home, lost and confused, his final few lines of narration stating that:

“When I got to the bed that night, it felt as if my legs had been broken. Or, at the very least, bent backwards.”

The second “white room” mention takes place at the very end of “The Creaking of the Seventh Step”, after Sara tries to tell Sensei about her and Sana’s “condition” (causing both his mind and the game immediately start to glitch out), which is then followed by six text-to-speech messages, collectively labeled within the game files as “words1-6”. The first five messages are reversed, just like the Old One’s lines in the recent Io event “The Hatchery”, and when properly processed spell out the following:

“And everything you know gets flipped on its head, like it was never yours to begin with. The world itself crumbles to dust, and all that’s left within it are the traces of who we once were. It becomes impossible to keep your eyes on what is important to you, when you see straight through everything. There were silhouettes with arms as wide as protocol, and a leg and a basket help the words when coming out alive. GET IT OUT IT’S INSIDE OF ME GET IT OUT GET IT OUT GIVE THIS ONE BACK (which is repeated four times).”

while the sixth one is spoken normally and with a notably different voice, with someone – almost certainly Pareidolia – directly addressing Akira and heavily chastising him for his actions:

“I warned you, and you didn’t listen. You never listen. Now more people have to get hurt. Are you happy? Stop looking for answers and go back into your box. The whitest of rooms will not wait for you when your head is halfway across the globe. Beneath you lies a promising future. Where are all of your dreams are as bright as emeralds. The creaking of the seventh step reminds you.”

And the final “white room” mention occurs in Chika’s Transpacific Sadness Symposium (which is technically also introduced in 0.47, same update as “WORMGOD54”, but whatever), with Amiokay speaking to Chika in reversed hexadecimal, which translates to

“We will take you and teach you to survive in this strange place you've found yourself in. And while you may not immediately agree, we can assure you that we are making the right choice. Each opportunity you have received to think for yourself has resulted in pain. And while pain may fuel you for the time being, there is a limit to what one person can take before turning into another. We ask that you join us in the White Room. We ask that you listen. We ask that you feel. Come. Take it. Live again.”

So, to summarize, it appears that the White Room is a universal “divine haven” of some kind that only a few select “chosen ones” are ever granted access to – perhaps a VIP lounge for the Gods and their most devout followers (which sort of lines up that one narration about “cottontails” and “the rating that determines how close we are to God” from “Sod in the Seedbed” – the same narration that is later intentionally interrupted and censored by USER2), or otherwise a high-level sanctuary that is likely able to protect you from even the upper echelons of threats within the Wishing Well. This could also give a potential reason as to why Nao-chan seemingly wasn’t able to perceive the room for what it actually was: she wasn’t granted the “right” to perceive it, and so to her it just looked like a normal interior of an old Japanese house.

Or maybe I’m completely wrong, and the “white room” that was mentioned by all of those characters is something entirely unrelated to what we saw in “WORMGOD54” – knowing how Selebus likes to write LiL, that is equally possible, too.

Continuing right from where we left off, some of you may have already noticed that all three events mentioning the “white room” that I referenced earlier had a certain unexpected common element between them – the very same element that I am now going to use to segue nicely into my next main topic of discussion: the apparent thematical connection between Tenchou, Amiokay and the concept of “things being backwards”.

Now, this is something that was *not* on my bingo card when I originally set out to write this post and, in fact, completely eluded me until I actually started looking through my notes in order to find some additional details on Tenchou and Amiokay and saw the evidence line up in a pretty convincing way, but looking back on it, I feel kind of disappointed with myself for (somehow?) never noticing the surprisingly high number of cases where two (or, sometimes, all three) of these outwardly unrelated links deliberately intersect. As they say: “twice is a coincidence, thrice is a pattern”.

The most obvious point of connection is definitely the abandoned school – the place where “some rules become bendable, while others stay the same” (according to Himawari) that has clear ties to both Amiokay, as she was crucified there in “The Letter T”, and Tenchou, since it is always snowing around there, regardless of the current season. Curiously, all four Happy Scenes that feature this abandoned school invariably include some form of Tenchou’s symbology (censored naked girl lying on the ground in front of a computer in “The Letter T”, cross being replaced with a tree in “Trinity Pt. I”, Maya mentioning the “computer god who is always watching with his roots planted in the ground” in “Baby Finches”, and the narrator saying “I am a tree now, and you are my roots” at the very end of “Arms Bent Back”), but the two events that directly contain Amiokay and/or the cross – “The Letter T” and “Arms Bent Back” – *also* have characters that speak backwards: Happy Ami in case of the former, and the aforementioned narrator in case of the latter.

To name a few other arguably circumstantial, but still fairly relevant examples of these thematic intersections, we have:

– The fact that Amiokay’s *only* non-Happy Scene appearance in all of Chapter 1 happens *specifically* in Yumi’s “I See You”, which is unlocked right after “This Town Has Two Halves” (an event that was, for all intents and purposes, explicitly orchestrated by Tenchou).

– Sensei briefly speaking backwards in the beginning of “Everything is Connected”: a Happy Scene that opens with an on-screen quote that references the final lines of both “The Letter T” and “How I Feel” events, which just so happen to prominently feature Amiokay. (There is also a secondary connection to her through “Nightvision” and “Turn Off the Lights”, though the degree in which Amiokay and Tenchou are actually involved in those two events compared to HOPE is… questionable, so I hesitate to list it here even as indirect proof.)

– Makoto’s “I'm Not Here” (in which Sensei is “pulled backwards” from HOPE by “invisible hands”, feeling “frayed wires wrapped around my ankles, scratching me enough to draw blood, but not enough to sever my Achilles tendons”).

– “Word of the Day” followed by “Backwards Dancing”: two events featuring very heavy presence of USER2, having him directly speak to Akira on multiple occasions and even “sharing the same screen” (according to the final narration line in the latter event), in addition to “Backwards Dancing” just in general having a lot of Tenchou-related symbology, like the snowy weather, static-covered sky or a gigantic tree randomly growing right in the middle of the school, making an entire wing of it completely inaccessible.

– “Things Like Stairs”, where Amiokay (or an angel impersonating her) appears in a scene directly referencing “Trinity Pt. II: Hell is Empty” (the one specifically about Tenchou), right as Sensei and Yuki are about to ascend the stairs to the second floor of Tojo Ramen and “learn the underlying truth of everything – what it means to live”.

– Ami’s “Somnambula” with its iconic “bus ride backwards”, which also notably includes a whole other slew of very curious details: the entire event having a secondary narrative throughline of USER 1 having trouble connecting (which he only actually manages to do *after* the event ends), Ami experiencing what can arguably be described as “visual alterations” at one point (something that is explicitly stated to be one of Tenchou’s abilities, while “the horny ball of light never learned how to do it”), and also the semi-final lines of “Somnambula” being “We get off the bus that’s moving backwards, and we *bend* ourselves until we wind up at our door.”, making a much more deliberate reference to the whole “bending back” motif.

– The aforementioned example from Chika’s TSS.

– Tsuneyo randomly speaking backwards for a couple of lines in her “Yamato Nadeshiko” (an event that directly precedes “WORMGOD54” and the introduction of the white room), which is then directly followed by her being mind-controlled by someone into repeating the whole “forced kiss on the bridge” scene – something that, just like back in Chapter 1 with Yumi, is heavily implied to be Tenchou’s doing.

– And to *really* stretch the “circumstantial” part of circumstantial evidence, there is also the whole thing with Amiokay being strongly associated with mirrors (something that is reiterated in both “Somewhere Far From Here” and “Rain King”, with the former even directly referencing the “bus ride backwards” from “Somnambula”), and what do mirrors do? They show things backwards.

(Though, curiously, in “Somewhere Far From Here” Yasu insists that these thoughts about “the loneliest girl, obscured behind the glass of 357 mirrors” (which is in itself a reference to “Hall of Mirrors”) do not come from HOPE, but are instead “an interference” from someone else, adding that “listening closely, I can hear the ocean” – which is pretty telling, all things considered, as amongst the members of the Trinity the one with the strongest connection to the ocean is, you guessed it, none other than Tenchou: it comes up in two previously brought up events, “I'm Not Here” (with the ocean “being unusually still” in contrast to the ground that is shaking due to HOPE’s appearance) and “Somnambula” (as a part of the quote “soon, the night will come, replacing the sun and shifting the tide, dragging many creatures into shallowest parts of the ocean, willing or not”); it comes up in Makoto’s “Rising of the Tide” (where Sensei is mysteriously compelled to make a move on Makoto and symbolizes this compulsion as “the ocean’s tide”, the entire situation just in general being extremely similar to what happens with Yumi in “This Town Has Two Halves”); it comes up in “Try. Try. Try.” (with Tsuneyo and the guy wearing purple baseball hat); and, of course, there is the Transpacific Sadness Symposium, which Amiokay is *also* clearly involved in, having appeared for three out of the nine girls so far.)

Finally, before I conclude this part and continue onto the next topic of on my list, I understand that there is one big elephant in the room that I need to address: the fact that Amiokay appears to be actively HOPE-aligned in many of her later Chapter 1 appearances, which effectively contradicts this entire interpretation of her being an agent of Tenchou (or otherwise connected to him in some way). To which I say – yes, you are correct, but I also potentially have an answer to this contradiction, even though it is, admittedly, a bit of a speculation on my part: the “Amiokay being forcefully converted by HOPE” theory.

Think of it this way: “The Room With Clocks” ends with Amiokay seemingly being captured by a group of angels – angels that, as far as we know, explicitly serve Nozomu and *only* Nozomu. Furthermore, as if that alone wasn’t enough to signify his involvement, during that very same scene Amiokay also warns Sensei that “its eyes are fake”, which, considering that Tenchou apparently doesn’t have any and Pareidolia wasn’t even in the picture yet, only really leaves one member of the Trinity (without even mentioning HOPE’s inherent symbolic connection to eyes, something that none of the other Gods share). The next time we see Amiokay in “The Letter T” she has been ritualistically crucified and left to suffer (with “AGAIN SHE LIVES – the answer you seek is HOPE” track repeatedly playing in the background), but the truly important detail here is that she also seemingly had her eyes taken away – something that can be clearly seen in both images of her staked to the cross. Then in “How I Feel” – which continues the trend of Amiokay being relentlessly tortured, just with pleasure this time instead of pain – her eyes have now been replaced with “angelic” swirly ones (except for when she and Sensei briefly teleport to the Room With Clocks), and she also has them for the majority of “Turn Off the Lights” (where Amiokay is acting very unlike herself, almost like she’s been brainwashed), only regaining her old eyes at the very end of that event. After that, Amiokay’s next and final Chapter 1 appearance happens in “Tick Tock Tick Tock Tick Tock” – the event that openly describes her as an “agent of HOPE” – and despite being back to looking fairly normal, the girl’s general demeanor and actions *do* seem to support that claim, in stark contrast to her earlier defiant disposition.

So what changed? Or, better question yet, is any of what I just said even remotely close to the truth? I don’t know! For all it’s worth, this entire theory could just be a whole bunch of nonsense that I randomly dreamt up in a bout of schizophrenic mania. Even if I’m completely off the mark, though, I *do* still believe that Amiokay’s original ideals (specifically, her words about “waking up” being the key to how we “open the door”, and the whole idea of “living to repair things” that she voices to Akira in “How I Feel”) align much more closely with Tenchou’s goals rather than Nozomu’s, not to mention that I find it kind of weird for HOPE to have *all* “alternative versions” of Maya at his side – it makes a lot more sense in my eyes for him to only be employing Youdidit and Moyo (who *are* more ideologically compatible with HOPE’s dogma), whereas Amiokay is closer to being a broken wildcard of sorts: a girl who is trapped in a cage of infinite mirrors and lost among the sea of her own reflections, no longer knowing whether she is authentic or a replica or aware of what her true beliefs even are.

Regardless, I’m fully done with this topic for now. It’s time to finally move on to something else – like Io’s giant hole!

Looking back on it, the sudden appearance of a massive sinkhole that unexpectedly swallowed Kumon-mi Academy can arguably be put up there as one of the most narrative-defining events in the entire game, as it was *that* single fallen domino that truly set everything in motion and heralded the total irreversible departure from Terminal 23’s boring and unchanging status quo: it caused Noriko to get transferred to Kumon-mi High and then promptly reunite with Sensei there, which then lead to him and Niki starting to reconnect with each other, which lead to Akira beginning to fully recover his memories, which lead to him remembering Sekai and her coming back to life, and so on – directly resulting in the insane mess of conflicting divine agendas and toxic inter-personal relationships we currently have in the story. So, with that preamble out of the way, what do we actually know about the sinkhole itself?

Well, aside from the fact that the whole incident just so happened to perfectly coincide with the second Reset and advent of Tenchou’s season, and that the school being swallowed was also pretty obviously orchestrated to happen specifically during the winter break so that no one who normally goes there would actually get hurt in the process… not much, really – with one notable exception. In Yasu’s very first character event, aptly named “The Hole That Swallowed Everything”, the girl mentions “not being allowed to talk about certain things in the Dorms, or else the floor will open up and swallow everything”. She then describes the fall of Kumon-mi Academy as “the reckoning”, and when Sensei asks her about it, Yasu replies with a single word: “slip” – calling it “an answer” that she’ll be able to share with him as soon as he “opens his eyes”. Later on, she also describes Sensei’s eyes as “tainted/purified” and refers to her sanctuary – the Church of New Hope – as “the place that cannot be swallowed by the hole that swallows everything”.

Now, *that* is pretty interesting, and only further points to Tenchou’s explicit involvement in this entire affair, but there is something *even more* interesting I would like to talk about next: the thematic dichotomy of “above and below” that, after playing a fairly major role throughout the first two Chapters and then seemingly taking a bit of a backseat in Chapter 3 and early Chapter 4, has now been fully reinstated into relevancy with repeated references to it in many of the recent updates featuring the sinkhole within the context of “something” existing/happening both over and under the city, like Tsubasa’s “When We Dead Awaken” (where the mysterious narrator says “I want to know what’s happening above and below. Where that massive hole leads to. How the town still breathes.”), or Io’s “The Hatchery” (where both the narrator and the Old One proclaim that “you do not want to know what lies beneath”, with the narrator also mentioning the sky as the second side of the same coin). Which, in turn, got me thinking about Yasu’s whole theory about multiple planes of existence that are stacked on top of each other – and, well, it all spiraled from there.

What if that hole in the ground leads to a different world – one that is not just a simple reflection of Kumon-mi, like we’ve seen in 0.45 and 0.53, but something completely alien and dangerous – and the reason why Yasu says “slip” as the answer to Sensei’s question is because that is literally what the sinkhole is: a “gate” that acts as a point of connection between two separate realities, which Akira has no need of, as he can already “slip” through dimensions? And, sure, the girl herself insistently claims that there is just one other plane of existence “lying directly on top of our current plane”, but this belief is later directly refuted by Nodoka in “Mille Crepe”, so maybe it’s a situation where Yasu only acknowledges one of them because that particular layer is somehow fundamentally related to HOPE while the other ones aren’t… or something.

Because if we presume that whatever lies at the bottom of that abyss *does* indeed pose great danger to the inhabitants of the city and/or the stability of Terminal 23 as a whole, then many of the previously odd and outwardly disjointed details begin to somewhat fall into place: like the aforementioned constant warnings of a “threat” that lurks beneath (something that even the narrator in “The Hatchery”, likely Nao, appears to be strongly apprehensive of – “greater things have greater fears” is the direct quote), or the line about how “somewhere in this city, there were creatures who had crawled their way free from a set of claws that kept them imprisoned behind bio-organic blades that only appeared indestructible” that gets said in “WORMGOD54”, or why the hole’s geographical location doesn’t seem to make any logical sense (if that is even the same hole at all, which Io seemingly doubts).

Furthermore, this “multiple worlds” interpretation could also help us better understand most of the other semi-related mysteries, such as:

– The beginning of “As The Sun Disappears”, where the narrator (likely Himawari) wonders whether “we will ever see it: the thing beneath us, the thing above – two sides of the same coin, cut in half and separated by more distance than one can travel in a lifetime”, arguing that “it will take far too long to become whole again; no matter what we do, we will always be just half of something” and admit to being scared – but also insist that “no one can know that – no one in the middle, at least”, though they will “reconsider their position once it’s somewhere else”.

– A certain line of narration from “The Creaking of the Seventh Step”, where Sensei says “There is something buried underneath our feet. It may very well swallow us whole.”.

– One particular tooltip from the “recalibration” sequence of “Girls Just Want to Have Fun” that states: “There is something buried underneath your feet. And something special in the sky!”

– The middle part of “Flora” – the one about “the sky opening” and “all that’s left is a hole” – that comes as a complete non-sequitur and doesn’t appear to be even remotely relevant to *anything* that happens either before or after it in that entire event.

– And on a more tangentially related note, how in “Endless Black (Sea of Nothing)”, while standing near the edge of the void he and Io have found, Sensei describes that he can “hear water, hear air – hear everything” while also pointing out the floating dust particles illuminated by “the light of the sun, falling endlessly from a separate abyss extending above” – the exact phenomenon that is repeatedly brought up in many events, including “Every Day I Grow Some More”, as “one of the things that I will never understand” – not to mention how it’s yet another nod towards duality of “above and beneath”, with two different abysses paralleling each other.

posts.content_text_full:
Welp, since I’m nothing if not dedicated to spending every waking moment of my life thinking about this unholy piece of fiction (to the point where I now get actual withdrawal symptoms from taking even a few days off from LiL), here it is – the thing that I mentioned I was working on about a week ago: an extensive (and at least somewhat comprehensive) list of all/most of the currently unresolved mysteries and plot threads that were directly brought back into relevancy over the course of the last ten updates – starting from the version 0.47 – presented (mostly) in a chronological order of their re-introduction into the spotlight.
Additionally, for the sake of actually talking about something different for once, I deliberately excluded all of the aforementioned mysteries and plot threads that are explicitly related to Ami, Maya, Himawari, Sekai (with a relatively small exception near the very end of the post) or the general workings of the Wishing Well, since I feel like these topics have already been mostly discussed to death by many people here – including me! – and I don’t want to just endlessly reiterate the same two or three talking points.
(PS: I once again had to split this post into two parts – with the second one coming out sometime later this week, whenever I feel like posting it – because I eventually realized that *literally no one* is going to read the whole 10000+ words at once, not to mention actually *process* them in full, so it would be better for me to separate them at least in half so as to not completely overwhelm people here. This way everyone who braves this wall of text will be able to properly sit on my proposed ideas for a couple of days, potentially coming up with their own additions and/or rebuttals to this analysis, which is more beneficial for the sake of having a constructive discussion.)
Spoiler:
The White Room
The first item on our list is the mystery of the second floor of Tojo Ramen: the strange pure-white room that Akira unexpectedly stumbles upon in “WORMGOD54” – a room that contains only a single unassuming metal door, presumably leading directly to Tenchou (implied via both WORMGOD’s narration about how “the door needs to be protected” and Tsuneyo’s later photo-guide of her room in “Defilement of a Temple”, where she says that “my father is the room right beside mine”), as well as a reference to the Upside-Down House (and/or the “there is something buried beneath our feet” line, but that is a subject for a later section) in the form of the cryptic wall graffiti.
Now, despite the fact that we’ve only actually seen this room as late as version 0.47, and the event that introduces it only raises multiple new questions without providing answers to any of the old ones, what some people might not be aware of is that the existence of this location was actually revealed to us all the way back in the very-very beginning of Chapter 3 – version 0.25pt2, to be exact – and it has been referenced *at least* three times even prior to its direct appearance in “WORMGOD54” by multiple meta-aware characters:
The very first mention of the so-called “white room” (presuming that I haven’t missed anything) happens in Yasu’s “Down The Rabbit Hole”, where she initially chastises Penemue for “barely touching his eggs”, since that means that he “won’t be able to come to the white room with us”, and then later – while experiencing what appears to be either a mental breakdown or a possession by some entity (likely HOPE) – begs Sensei to also “partake in their feast that transcends time itself” by eating one of Penemue eggs and thus “reserve your space in the white room”, because “there is nowhere else that can protect us from…” something, though the girl is unable to finish her sentence due to an especially severe bout of headache. The event then concludes with the entire tea party seemingly being completely retconned from existence (*or* an implication that it all took place in Akira’s head, explaining why everyone suddenly “disappeared” and why Yasu recounts a completely different version of these events in her “Sore Thumb”) and Sensei going back home, lost and confused, his final few lines of narration stating that:
“When I got to the bed that night, it felt as if my legs had been broken. Or, at the very least, bent backwards.”
The second “white room” mention takes place at the very end of “The Creaking of the Seventh Step”, after Sara tries to tell Sensei about her and Sana’s “condition” (causing both his mind and the game immediately start to glitch out), which is then followed by six text-to-speech messages, collectively labeled within the game files as “words1-6”. The first five messages are reversed, just like the Old One’s lines in the recent Io event “The Hatchery”, and when properly processed spell out the following:
“And everything you know gets flipped on its head, like it was never yours to begin with. The world itself crumbles to dust, and all that’s left within it are the traces of who we once were. It becomes impossible to keep your eyes on what is important to you, when you see straight through everything. There were silhouettes with arms as wide as protocol, and a leg and a basket help the words when coming out alive. GET IT OUT IT’S INSIDE OF ME GET IT OUT GET IT OUT GIVE THIS ONE BACK (which is repeated four times).”
while the sixth one is spoken normally and with a notably different voice, with someone – almost certainly Pareidolia – directly addressing Akira and heavily chastising him for his actions:
“I warned you, and you didn’t listen. You never listen. Now more people have to get hurt. Are you happy? Stop looking for answers and go back into your box. The whitest of rooms will not wait for you when your head is halfway across the globe. Beneath you lies a promising future. Where are all of your dreams are as bright as emeralds. The creaking of the seventh step reminds you.”
And the final “white room” mention occurs in Chika’s Transpacific Sadness Symposium (which is technically also introduced in 0.47, same update as “WORMGOD54”, but whatever), with Amiokay speaking to Chika in reversed hexadecimal, which translates to
“We will take you and teach you to survive in this strange place you've found yourself in. And while you may not immediately agree, we can assure you that we are making the right choice. Each opportunity you have received to think for yourself has resulted in pain. And while pain may fuel you for the time being, there is a limit to what one person can take before turning into another. We ask that you join us in the White Room. We ask that you listen. We ask that you feel. Come. Take it. Live again.”
So, to summarize, it appears that the White Room is a universal “divine haven” of some kind that only a few select “chosen ones” are ever granted access to – perhaps a VIP lounge for the Gods and their most devout followers (which sort of lines up that one narration about “cottontails” and “the rating that determines how close we are to God” from “Sod in the Seedbed” – the same narration that is later intentionally interrupted and censored by USER2), or otherwise a high-level sanctuary that is likely able to protect you from even the upper echelons of threats within the Wishing Well. This could also give a potential reason as to why Nao-chan seemingly wasn’t able to perceive the room for what it actually was: she wasn’t granted the “right” to perceive it, and so to her it just looked like a normal interior of an old Japanese house.
Or maybe I’m completely wrong, and the “white room” that was mentioned by all of those characters is something entirely unrelated to what we saw in “WORMGOD54” – knowing how Selebus likes to write LiL, that is equally possible, too.
Spoiler:
The Wire God and Amiokay (amongst other things)
Continuing right from where we left off, some of you may have already noticed that all three events mentioning the “white room” that I referenced earlier had a certain unexpected common element between them – the very same element that I am now going to use to segue nicely into my next main topic of discussion: the apparent thematical connection between Tenchou, Amiokay and the concept of “things being backwards”.
Now, this is something that was *not* on my bingo card when I originally set out to write this post and, in fact, completely eluded me until I actually started looking through my notes in order to find some additional details on Tenchou and Amiokay and saw the evidence line up in a pretty convincing way, but looking back on it, I feel kind of disappointed with myself for (somehow?) never noticing the surprisingly high number of cases where two (or, sometimes, all three) of these outwardly unrelated links deliberately intersect. As they say: “twice is a coincidence, thrice is a pattern”.
The most obvious point of connection is definitely the abandoned school – the place where “some rules become bendable, while others stay the same” (according to Himawari) that has clear ties to both Amiokay, as she was crucified there in “The Letter T”, and Tenchou, since it is always snowing around there, regardless of the current season. Curiously, all four Happy Scenes that feature this abandoned school invariably include some form of Tenchou’s symbology (censored naked girl lying on the ground in front of a computer in “The Letter T”, cross being replaced with a tree in “Trinity Pt. I”, Maya mentioning the “computer god who is always watching with his roots planted in the ground” in “Baby Finches”, and the narrator saying “I am a tree now, and you are my roots” at the very end of “Arms Bent Back”), but the two events that directly contain Amiokay and/or the cross – “The Letter T” and “Arms Bent Back” – *also* have characters that speak backwards: Happy Ami in case of the former, and the aforementioned narrator in case of the latter.
To name a few other arguably circumstantial, but still fairly relevant examples of these thematic intersections, we have:
– The fact that Amiokay’s *only* non-Happy Scene appearance in all of Chapter 1 happens *specifically* in Yumi’s “I See You”, which is unlocked right after “This Town Has Two Halves” (an event that was, for all intents and purposes, explicitly orchestrated by Tenchou).
– Sensei briefly speaking backwards in the beginning of “Everything is Connected”: a Happy Scene that opens with an on-screen quote that references the final lines of both “The Letter T” and “How I Feel” events, which just so happen to prominently feature Amiokay. (There is also a secondary connection to her through “Nightvision” and “Turn Off the Lights”, though the degree in which Amiokay and Tenchou are actually involved in those two events compared to HOPE is… questionable, so I hesitate to list it here even as indirect proof.)
– Makoto’s “I'm Not Here” (in which Sensei is “pulled backwards” from HOPE by “invisible hands”, feeling “frayed wires wrapped around my ankles, scratching me enough to draw blood, but not enough to sever my Achilles tendons”).
– “Word of the Day” followed by “Backwards Dancing”: two events featuring very heavy presence of USER2, having him directly speak to Akira on multiple occasions and even “sharing the same screen” (according to the final narration line in the latter event), in addition to “Backwards Dancing” just in general having a lot of Tenchou-related symbology, like the snowy weather, static-covered sky or a gigantic tree randomly growing right in the middle of the school, making an entire wing of it completely inaccessible.
– “Things Like Stairs”, where Amiokay (or an angel impersonating her) appears in a scene directly referencing “Trinity Pt. II: Hell is Empty” (the one specifically about Tenchou), right as Sensei and Yuki are about to ascend the stairs to the second floor of Tojo Ramen and “learn the underlying truth of everything – what it means to live”.
– Ami’s “Somnambula” with its iconic “bus ride backwards”, which also notably includes a whole other slew of very curious details: the entire event having a secondary narrative throughline of USER 1 having trouble connecting (which he only actually manages to do *after* the event ends), Ami experiencing what can arguably be described as “visual alterations” at one point (something that is explicitly stated to be one of Tenchou’s abilities, while “the horny ball of light never learned how to do it”), and also the semi-final lines of “Somnambula” being “We get off the bus that’s moving backwards, and we *bend* ourselves until we wind up at our door.”, making a much more deliberate reference to the whole “bending back” motif.
– The aforementioned example from Chika’s TSS.
– Tsuneyo randomly speaking backwards for a couple of lines in her “Yamato Nadeshiko” (an event that directly precedes “WORMGOD54” and the introduction of the white room), which is then directly followed by her being mind-controlled by someone into repeating the whole “forced kiss on the bridge” scene – something that, just like back in Chapter 1 with Yumi, is heavily implied to be Tenchou’s doing.
– And to *really* stretch the “circumstantial” part of circumstantial evidence, there is also the whole thing with Amiokay being strongly associated with mirrors (something that is reiterated in both “Somewhere Far From Here” and “Rain King”, with the former even directly referencing the “bus ride backwards” from “Somnambula”), and what do mirrors do? They show things backwards.
(Though, curiously, in “Somewhere Far From Here” Yasu insists that these thoughts about “the loneliest girl, obscured behind the glass of 357 mirrors” (which is in itself a reference to “Hall of Mirrors”) do not come from HOPE, but are instead “an interference” from someone else, adding that “listening closely, I can hear the ocean” – which is pretty telling, all things considered, as amongst the members of the Trinity the one with the strongest connection to the ocean is, you guessed it, none other than Tenchou: it comes up in two previously brought up events, “I'm Not Here” (with the ocean “being unusually still” in contrast to the ground that is shaking due to HOPE’s appearance) and “Somnambula” (as a part of the quote “soon, the night will come, replacing the sun and shifting the tide, dragging many creatures into shallowest parts of the ocean, willing or not”); it comes up in Makoto’s “Rising of the Tide” (where Sensei is mysteriously compelled to make a move on Makoto and symbolizes this compulsion as “the ocean’s tide”, the entire situation just in general being extremely similar to what happens with Yumi in “This Town Has Two Halves”); it comes up in “Try. Try. Try.” (with Tsuneyo and the guy wearing purple baseball hat); and, of course, there is the Transpacific Sadness Symposium, which Amiokay is *also* clearly involved in, having appeared for three out of the nine girls so far.)
Finally, before I conclude this part and continue onto the next topic of on my list, I understand that there is one big elephant in the room that I need to address: the fact that Amiokay appears to be actively HOPE-aligned in many of her later Chapter 1 appearances, which effectively contradicts this entire interpretation of her being an agent of Tenchou (or otherwise connected to him in some way). To which I say – yes, you are correct, but I also potentially have an answer to this contradiction, even though it is, admittedly, a bit of a speculation on my part: the “Amiokay being forcefully converted by HOPE” theory.
Think of it this way: “The Room With Clocks” ends with Amiokay seemingly being captured by a group of angels – angels that, as far as we know, explicitly serve Nozomu and *only* Nozomu. Furthermore, as if that alone wasn’t enough to signify his involvement, during that very same scene Amiokay also warns Sensei that “its eyes are fake”, which, considering that Tenchou apparently doesn’t have any and Pareidolia wasn’t even in the picture yet, only really leaves one member of the Trinity (without even mentioning HOPE’s inherent symbolic connection to eyes, something that none of the other Gods share). The next time we see Amiokay in “The Letter T” she has been ritualistically crucified and left to suffer (with “AGAIN SHE LIVES – the answer you seek is HOPE” track repeatedly playing in the background), but the truly important detail here is that she also seemingly had her eyes taken away – something that can be clearly seen in both images of her staked to the cross. Then in “How I Feel” – which continues the trend of Amiokay being relentlessly tortured, just with pleasure this time instead of pain – her eyes have now been replaced with “angelic” swirly ones (except for when she and Sensei briefly teleport to the Room With Clocks), and she also has them for the majority of “Turn Off the Lights” (where Amiokay is acting very unlike herself, almost like she’s been brainwashed), only regaining her old eyes at the very end of that event. After that, Amiokay’s next and final Chapter 1 appearance happens in “Tick Tock Tick Tock Tick Tock” – the event that openly describes her as an “agent of HOPE” – and despite being back to looking fairly normal, the girl’s general demeanor and actions *do* seem to support that claim, in stark contrast to her earlier defiant disposition.
So what changed? Or, better question yet, is any of what I just said even remotely close to the truth? I don’t know! For all it’s worth, this entire theory could just be a whole bunch of nonsense that I randomly dreamt up in a bout of schizophrenic mania. Even if I’m completely off the mark, though, I *do* still believe that Amiokay’s original ideals (specifically, her words about “waking up” being the key to how we “open the door”, and the whole idea of “living to repair things” that she voices to Akira in “How I Feel”) align much more closely with Tenchou’s goals rather than Nozomu’s, not to mention that I find it kind of weird for HOPE to have *all* “alternative versions” of Maya at his side – it makes a lot more sense in my eyes for him to only be employing Youdidit and Moyo (who *are* more ideologically compatible with HOPE’s dogma), whereas Amiokay is closer to being a broken wildcard of sorts: a girl who is trapped in a cage of infinite mirrors and lost among the sea of her own reflections, no longer knowing whether she is authentic or a replica or aware of what her true beliefs even are.
Regardless, I’m fully done with this topic for now. It’s time to finally move on to something else – like Io’s giant hole!
Spoiler:

Looking back on it, the sudden appearance of a massive sinkhole that unexpectedly swallowed Kumon-mi Academy can arguably be put up there as one of the most narrative-defining events in the entire game, as it was *that* single fallen domino that truly set everything in motion and heralded the total irreversible departure from Terminal 23’s boring and unchanging status quo: it caused Noriko to get transferred to Kumon-mi High and then promptly reunite with Sensei there, which then lead to him and Niki starting to reconnect with each other, which lead to Akira beginning to fully recover his memories, which lead to him remembering Sekai and her coming back to life, and so on – directly resulting in the insane mess of conflicting divine agendas and toxic inter-personal relationships we currently have in the story. spoilers.title: The Wire God and Amiokay (amongst other things)
spoilers.html:
Continuing right from where we left off, some of you may have already noticed that all three events mentioning the “white room” that I referenced earlier had a certain unexpected common element between them – the very same element that I am now going to use to segue nicely into my next main topic of discussion: the apparent thematical connection between Tenchou, Amiokay and the concept of “things being backwards”.

Now, this is something that was *not* on my bingo card when I originally set out to write this post and, in fact, completely eluded me until I actually started looking through my notes in order to find some additional details on Tenchou and Amiokay and saw the evidence line up in a pretty convincing way, but looking back on it, I feel kind of disappointed with myself for (somehow?) never noticing the surprisingly high number of cases where two (or, sometimes, all three) of these outwardly unrelated links deliberately intersect. As they say: “twice is a coincidence, thrice is a pattern”.

The most obvious point of connection is definitely the abandoned school – the place where “some rules become bendable, while others stay the same” (according to Himawari) that has clear ties to both Amiokay, as she was crucified there in “The Letter T”, and Tenchou, since it is always snowing around there, regardless of the current season. Curiously, all four Happy Scenes that feature this abandoned school invariably include some form of Tenchou’s symbology (censored naked girl lying on the ground in front of a computer in “The Letter T”, cross being replaced with a tree in “Trinity Pt. I”, Maya mentioning the “computer god who is always watching with his roots planted in the ground” in “Baby Finches”, and the narrator saying “I am a tree now, and you are my roots” at the very end of “Arms Bent Back”), but the two events that directly contain Amiokay and/or the cross – “The Letter T” and “Arms Bent Back” – *also* have characters that speak backwards: Happy Ami in case of the former, and the aforementioned narrator in case of the latter.

To name a few other arguably circumstantial, but still fairly relevant examples of these thematic intersections, we have:

– The fact that Amiokay’s *only* non-Happy Scene appearance in all of Chapter 1 happens *specifically* in Yumi’s “I See You”, which is unlocked right after “This Town Has Two Halves” (an event that was, for all intents and purposes, explicitly orchestrated by Tenchou).

– Sensei briefly speaking backwards in the beginning of “Everything is Connected”: a Happy Scene that opens with an on-screen quote that references the final lines of both “The Letter T” and “How I Feel” events, which just so happen to prominently feature Amiokay. (There is also a secondary connection to her through “Nightvision” and “Turn Off the Lights”, though the degree in which Amiokay and Tenchou are actually involved in those two events compared to HOPE is… questionable, so I hesitate to list it here even as indirect proof.)

– Makoto’s “I'm Not Here” (in which Sensei is “pulled backwards” from HOPE by “invisible hands”, feeling “frayed wires wrapped around my ankles, scratching me enough to draw blood, but not enough to sever my Achilles tendons”).

– “Word of the Day” followed by “Backwards Dancing”: two events featuring very heavy presence of USER2, having him directly speak to Akira on multiple occasions and even “sharing the same screen” (according to the final narration line in the latter event), in addition to “Backwards Dancing” just in general having a lot of Tenchou-related symbology, like the snowy weather, static-covered sky or a gigantic tree randomly growing right in the middle of the school, making an entire wing of it completely inaccessible.

– “Things Like Stairs”, where Amiokay (or an angel impersonating her) appears in a scene directly referencing “Trinity Pt. II: Hell is Empty” (the one specifically about Tenchou), right as Sensei and Yuki are about to ascend the stairs to the second floor of Tojo Ramen and “learn the underlying truth of everything – what it means to live”.

– Ami’s “Somnambula” with its iconic “bus ride backwards”, which also notably includes a whole other slew of very curious details: the entire event having a secondary narrative throughline of USER 1 having trouble connecting (which he only actually manages to do *after* the event ends), Ami experiencing what can arguably be described as “visual alterations” at one point (something that is explicitly stated to be one of Tenchou’s abilities, while “the horny ball of light never learned how to do it”), and also the semi-final lines of “Somnambula” being “We get off the bus that’s moving backwards, and we *bend* ourselves until we wind up at our door.”, making a much more deliberate reference to the whole “bending back” motif.

– The aforementioned example from Chika’s TSS.

– Tsuneyo randomly speaking backwards for a couple of lines in her “Yamato Nadeshiko” (an event that directly precedes “WORMGOD54” and the introduction of the white room), which is then directly followed by her being mind-controlled by someone into repeating the whole “forced kiss on the bridge” scene – something that, just like back in Chapter 1 with Yumi, is heavily implied to be Tenchou’s doing.

– And to *really* stretch the “circumstantial” part of circumstantial evidence, there is also the whole thing with Amiokay being strongly associated with mirrors (something that is reiterated in both “Somewhere Far From Here” and “Rain King”, with the former even directly referencing the “bus ride backwards” from “Somnambula”), and what do mirrors do? They show things backwards.

(Though, curiously, in “Somewhere Far From Here” Yasu insists that these thoughts about “the loneliest girl, obscured behind the glass of 357 mirrors” (which is in itself a reference to “Hall of Mirrors”) do not come from HOPE, but are instead “an interference” from someone else, adding that “listening closely, I can hear the ocean” – which is pretty telling, all things considered, as amongst the members of the Trinity the one with the strongest connection to the ocean is, you guessed it, none other than Tenchou: it comes up in two previously brought up events, “I'm Not Here” (with the ocean “being unusually still” in contrast to the ground that is shaking due to HOPE’s appearance) and “Somnambula” (as a part of the quote “soon, the night will come, replacing the sun and shifting the tide, dragging many creatures into shallowest parts of the ocean, willing or not”); it comes up in Makoto’s “Rising of the Tide” (where Sensei is mysteriously compelled to make a move on Makoto and symbolizes this compulsion as “the ocean’s tide”, the entire situation just in general being extremely similar to what happens with Yumi in “This Town Has Two Halves”); it comes up in “Try. Try. Try.” (with Tsuneyo and the guy wearing purple baseball hat); and, of course, there is the Transpacific Sadness Symposium, which Amiokay is *also* clearly involved in, having appeared for three out of the nine girls so far.)

Finally, before I conclude this part and continue onto the next topic of on my list, I understand that there is one big elephant in the room that I need to address: the fact that Amiokay appears to be actively HOPE-aligned in many of her later Chapter 1 appearances, which effectively contradicts this entire interpretation of her being an agent of Tenchou (or otherwise connected to him in some way). To which I say – yes, you are correct, but I also potentially have an answer to this contradiction, even though it is, admittedly, a bit of a speculation on my part: the “Amiokay being forcefully converted by HOPE” theory.

Think of it this way: “The Room With Clocks” ends with Amiokay seemingly being captured by a group of angels – angels that, as far as we know, explicitly serve Nozomu and *only* Nozomu. Furthermore, as if that alone wasn’t enough to signify his involvement, during that very same scene Amiokay also warns Sensei that “its eyes are fake”, which, considering that Tenchou apparently doesn’t have any and Pareidolia wasn’t even in the picture yet, only really leaves one member of the Trinity (without even mentioning HOPE’s inherent symbolic connection to eyes, something that none of the other Gods share). The next time we see Amiokay in “The Letter T” she has been ritualistically crucified and left to suffer (with “AGAIN SHE LIVES – the answer you seek is HOPE” track repeatedly playing in the background), but the truly important detail here is that she also seemingly had her eyes taken away – something that can be clearly seen in both images of her staked to the cross. Then in “How I Feel” – which continues the trend of Amiokay being relentlessly tortured, just with pleasure this time instead of pain – her eyes have now been replaced with “angelic” swirly ones (except for when she and Sensei briefly teleport to the Room With Clocks), and she also has them for the majority of “Turn Off the Lights” (where Amiokay is acting very unlike herself, almost like she’s been brainwashed), only regaining her old eyes at the very end of that event. After that, Amiokay’s next and final Chapter 1 appearance happens in “Tick Tock Tick Tock Tick Tock” – the event that openly describes her as an “agent of HOPE” – and despite being back to looking fairly normal, the girl’s general demeanor and actions *do* seem to support that claim, in stark contrast to her earlier defiant disposition.

So what changed? Or, better question yet, is any of what I just said even remotely close to the truth? I don’t know! For all it’s worth, this entire theory could just be a whole bunch of nonsense that I randomly dreamt up in a bout of schizophrenic mania. Even if I’m completely off the mark, though, I *do* still believe that Amiokay’s original ideals (specifically, her words about “waking up” being the key to how we “open the door”, and the whole idea of “living to repair things” that she voices to Akira in “How I Feel”) align much more closely with Tenchou’s goals rather than Nozomu’s, not to mention that I find it kind of weird for HOPE to have *all* “alternative versions” of Maya at his side – it makes a lot more sense in my eyes for him to only be employing Youdidit and Moyo (who *are* more ideologically compatible with HOPE’s dogma), whereas Amiokay is closer to being a broken wildcard of sorts: a girl who is trapped in a cage of infinite mirrors and lost among the sea of her own reflections, no longer knowing whether she is authentic or a replica or aware of what her true beliefs even are.

Regardless, I’m fully done with this topic for now. It’s time to finally move on to something else – like Io’s giant hole!

spoilers.title: The Sinkhole (and Kumon-mi’s other geographic mysteries)
spoilers.html:
Looking back on it, the sudden appearance of a massive sinkhole that unexpectedly swallowed Kumon-mi Academy can arguably be put up there as one of the most narrative-defining events in the entire game, as it was *that* single fallen domino that truly set everything in motion and heralded the total irreversible departure from Terminal 23’s boring and unchanging status quo: it caused Noriko to get transferred to Kumon-mi High and then promptly reunite with Sensei there, which then lead to him and Niki starting to reconnect with each other, which lead to Akira beginning to fully recover his memories, which lead to him remembering Sekai and her coming back to life, and so on – directly resulting in the insane mess of conflicting divine agendas and toxic inter-personal relationships we currently have in the story. So, with that preamble out of the way, what do we actually know about the sinkhole itself?

Well, aside from the fact that the whole incident just so happened to perfectly coincide with the second Reset and advent of Tenchou’s season, and that the school being swallowed was also pretty obviously orchestrated to happen specifically during the winter break so that no one who normally goes there would actually get hurt in the process… not much, really – with one notable exception. In Yasu’s very first character event, aptly named “The Hole That Swallowed Everything”, the girl mentions “not being allowed to talk about certain things in the Dorms, or else the floor will open up and swallow everything”. She then describes the fall of Kumon-mi Academy as “the reckoning”, and when Sensei asks her about it, Yasu replies with a single word: “slip” – calling it “an answer” that she’ll be able to share with him as soon as he “opens his eyes”. Later on, she also describes Sensei’s eyes as “tainted/purified” and refers to her sanctuary – the Church of New Hope – as “the place that cannot be swallowed by the hole that swallows everything”.

Now, *that* is pretty interesting, and only further points to Tenchou’s explicit involvement in this entire affair, but there is something *even more* interesting I would like to talk about next: the thematic dichotomy of “above and below” that, after playing a fairly major role throughout the first two Chapters and then seemingly taking a bit of a backseat in Chapter 3 and early Chapter 4, has now been fully reinstated into relevancy with repeated references to it in many of the recent updates featuring the sinkhole within the context of “something” existing/happening both over and under the city, like Tsubasa’s “When We Dead Awaken” (where the mysterious narrator says “I want to know what’s happening above and below. Where that massive hole leads to. How the town still breathes.”), or Io’s “The Hatchery” (where both the narrator and the Old One proclaim that “you do not want to know what lies beneath”, with the narrator also mentioning the sky as the second side of the same coin). Which, in turn, got me thinking about Yasu’s whole theory about multiple planes of existence that are stacked on top of each other – and, well, it all spiraled from there.

What if that hole in the ground leads to a different world – one that is not just a simple reflection of Kumon-mi, like we’ve seen in 0.45 and 0.53, but something completely alien and dangerous – and the reason why Yasu says “slip” as the answer to Sensei’s question is because that is literally what the sinkhole is: a “gate” that acts as a point of connection between two separate realities, which Akira has no need of, as he can already “slip” through dimensions? And, sure, the girl herself insistently claims that there is just one other plane of existence “lying directly on top of our current plane”, but this belief is later directly refuted by Nodoka in “Mille Crepe”, so maybe it’s a situation where Yasu only acknowledges one of them because that particular layer is somehow fundamentally related to HOPE while the other ones aren’t… or something.

Because if we presume that whatever lies at the bottom of that abyss *does* indeed pose great danger to the inhabitants of the city and/or the stability of Terminal 23 as a whole, then many of the previously odd and outwardly disjointed details begin to somewhat fall into place: like the aforementioned constant warnings of a “threat” that lurks beneath (something that even the narrator in “The Hatchery”, likely Nao, appears to be strongly apprehensive of – “greater things have greater fears” is the direct quote), or the line about how “somewhere in this city, there were creatures who had crawled their way free from a set of claws that kept them imprisoned behind bio-organic blades that only appeared indestructible” that gets said in “WORMGOD54”, or why the hole’s geographical location doesn’t seem to make any logical sense (if that is even the same hole at all, which Io seemingly doubts).

Furthermore, this “multiple worlds” interpretation could also help us better understand most of the other semi-related mysteries, such as:

– The beginning of “As The Sun Disappears”, where the narrator (likely Himawari) wonders whether “we will ever see it: the thing beneath us, the thing above – two sides of the same coin, cut in half and separated by more distance than one can travel in a lifetime”, arguing that “it will take far too long to become whole again; no matter what we do, we will always be just half of something” and admit to being scared – but also insist that “no one can know that – no one in the middle, at least”, though they will “reconsider their position once it’s somewhere else”.

– A certain line of narration from “The Creaking of the Seventh Step”, where Sensei says “There is something buried underneath our feet. It may very well swallow us whole.”.

– One particular tooltip from the “recalibration” sequence of “Girls Just Want to Have Fun” that states: “There is something buried underneath your feet. And something special in the sky!”

– The middle part of “Flora” – the one about “the sky opening” and “all that’s left is a hole” – that comes as a complete non-sequitur and doesn’t appear to be even remotely relevant to *anything* that happens either before or after it in that entire event.

– And on a more tangentially related note, how in “Endless Black (Sea of Nothing)”, while standing near the edge of the void he and Io have found, Sensei describes that he can “hear water, hear air – hear everything” while also pointing out the floating dust particles illuminated by “the light of the sun, falling endlessly from a separate abyss extending above” – the exact phenomenon that is repeatedly brought up in many events, including “Every Day I Grow Some More”, as “one of the things that I will never understand” – not to mention how it’s yet another nod towards duality of “above and beneath”, with two different abysses paralleling each other.

Finally, there are a few other enigmatic places in Kumon-mi that likewise deserve their own mention, like the Dorms building (a half-finished liminal space with infinite floors, “yet we only use three of them” according to Uta in “Heebie-Jeebies”), the iconic sidewalk that randomly ends in an endless abyss (a thing that Ami is well aware of, by the way, as revealed in “Double Jeopardy”) that was recently featured in a scene chosen by Selebus for the 0.57 title card, or the sprawling underground tunnels (which are effectively alive and ever-changing, just like the city itself, in addition to likely being tied to that very same sidewalk based on “Where the Sidewalk Ends”), directly referenced just a few updates ago by the narrator – probably Nao – in “The Hatchery”, in the context of them “having asked for a castle” and instead “only receiving a tunnel”.
spoilers.text:
Looking back on it, the sudden appearance of a massive sinkhole that unexpectedly swallowed Kumon-mi Academy can arguably be put up there as one of the most narrative-defining events in the entire game, as it was *that* single fallen domino that truly set everything in motion and heralded the total irreversible departure from Terminal 23’s boring and unchanging status quo: it caused Noriko to get transferred to Kumon-mi High and then promptly reunite with Sensei there, which then lead to him and Niki starting to reconnect with each other, which lead to Akira beginning to fully recover his memories, which lead to him remembering Sekai and her coming back to life, and so on – directly resulting in the insane mess of conflicting divine agendas and toxic inter-personal relationships we currently have in the story. So, with that preamble out of the way, what do we actually know about the sinkhole itself?
Well, aside from the fact that the whole incident just so happened to perfectly coincide with the second Reset and advent of Tenchou’s season, and that the school being swallowed was also pretty obviously orchestrated to happen specifically during the winter break so that no one who normally goes there would actually get hurt in the process… not much, really – with one notable exception. posts.content_html_raw:
Back during 0.54 I had a big lightbulb moment, letting me piece together three related theories about the Nagasawas. Now that I have some time to write about something other than the most recent update, I'll be sharing these as three separate posts.

The theory I am arguing for in part 1: Much like Maya, Nodoka Nagasawa isn't a real girl - she's Kyoko Nagasawa's wish.
Foreshadowing! Nodoka comes from the wishing well.
Nodoka herself has described how she came into existence from nothing. She wasn't a thought before her existence, because the first thought of her was the wish that created her.
She also said she has no father and was made in a "tube".

Her reference to a tube is phrased as a hypothetical/joke, but Kyoko used the same term in 0.54. (Yes, this is Kyoko speaking to Nodoka. I'll talk about it in a later post.)
And someone else who knows Kyoko interrupted Sensei's thoughts to call Nodoka "someone that should not exist", echoing the language Sekai and Pareidolia have used about wish girl Maya.

(Note: alternatively, this passage could be read as saying that Kyoko is the girl who shouldn't exist, but Nodoka fits much better given the other clues)
The bit about Nodoka's eyes leads into the next section.
Despite being a wish, Nodoka inherited her appearance from two people. She looks very similar to Kyoko, but with someone else's eyes. I argue that this other person is Yuko, the lavender-haired girl in the upside down house whom Kyoko is in love/obsessed with.
Nodoka looks so much like a young Kyoko that Shiori thought she was Kyoko, at least momentarily.
There's one exception though: Shiori can't see Nodoka's eyes. Nodoka doesn't have Kyoko's eyes, she has the same eyes as whoever was speaking to Kyoko in "Taint the Sapling".
Let's try to identify who this mystery person is. To start with the obvious, we haven't seen anyone in the game that has the same eye color as Nodoka, including Akira (in flashbacks his eyes are grey).

The mystery person probably has some connection to the upside down house. They know Kyoko, and when they start talking there's a photograph of the interior of a house. We've been shown the inside of the upside down house (or at least an allusion to it) as a photograph before.
The speaker also mentions finding black and pink hairs. Two of the upside down house residents, Shiori and Ai, have those hair colors (see this post).

One of the girls in the upside down house is unknown to Sensei, but has eyes that he recognizes. Maybe because he's seen the same eyes on Nodoka.
I think the "Taint the Sapling" speaker is probably one of the house's other residents. She's talking to Kyoko, so it's not her. It's probably not Shiori or Ai, because they wouldn't care about finding their own hair. That leaves Setsuna and Yuko; of the two Yuko is far more important to Kyoko. Kyoko is obsessed with her, with a particular fixation on her hair.
We can even check if Yuko has the right eye color, as we've seen her... sort of. In "Excerpt from a Waterlogged Journal", the character DOUBT is an artistic representation of Yuko, complete with hair of literal lavender. We can't say anything definitive about her true eye color, but it's not unreasonable that it's the same as Nodoka's.

(Please note that I'm not saying this is positive evidence, only that it would be very easy for it to be negative evidence if her eyes were shown as sapphires or something.)
My theory is that Nodoka shares a resemblance with these two "parents" because of how she was created: Kyoko wished that she and Yuko had a daughter.
Other wishes we know about (Maya and especially Nao) don't look like their "parents", so there must be some reason that Nodoka does. As we'll see shortly, Kyoko dreamed about having a daughter, but knew it would never happen. For one, she's a lesbian (probably exclusively) and can't have a child of her body with another girl. Second, her love for Yuko was probably unrequited, based on "Lavender" and "An Excerpt from a Waterlogged Journal". The only way she could make her daughter a reality was by wishing for her.

Yuko's interjection in "Taint the Sapling" also supports the idea that Kyoko is solely responsible for Nodoka's existence. Although Nodoka has her eyes, she only thinks of her as "[Kyoko's] daughter" rather than "our daughter". (This still follows even if you don't buy the Yuko theory; the speaker has a distance from Nodoka that seems contrary to their shared genes.)

The evidence for Kyoko's thoughts come from a series of tweets at @AreYouHappyHere (I don't love that we have to go outside of the game for clues, but since they're there I'm going to use them). I think these show Kyoko's growing desires that led her to wish for Nodoka long before the start of the game. Most of the tweets don't identify the speaker and many only speak of a cryptic "her" rather than a daughter, but I think there's enough commonalities between them to conclude this is one speaker thinking about one "her", which means it must be Kyoko thinking about her daughter.

To begin with, let's establish that Kyoko has no memories from before the house. If Nodoka is her real daughter who she had before getting stuck in the house, she shouldn't know about her.

"it was probably nicer when I was a little girl / i asked the others about their memories from when they weren't here, / but they were all in the same boat / it's just that this boat is actually a house, and not remembering / anything else probably makes things better for me in the long run"
Despite this, she continually thinks about her daughter. At first it's abstract and hypothetical.
She wonders about her daughter's eye color while speaking to Yuko, linking the two.

"help me, yXXXXX" (y[uko]) and "i wonder if i had a child if she would have my eyes"
The daughter she's thinking about isn't only hers - she imagines the daughter that we will never have. She wants to have a daughter with someone specific. She has never shown any interest in men and Yuko is the one she loves.

(The "favorite couple" is probably Shiori and Ai)
Over time her thoughts take the form of dreams that feel as real as her missing memories.

"Each dream I have brings me closer to her" and "Yuko tells me I am going insane." and "Why am I the only one with memories like these?"
And she knows that her daughter's name is Nodoka. But she's worried that Nodoka is only something she dreamed up, rather than someone that actually exists.

An alternate explanation for these tweets is that Nodoka always existed outside the house, and Kyoko was recovering lost memories of her. I don't think the timeline works, though, because I think Kyoko's mind has been stuck in the house since she was quite young. Her tweets sound like a teen or young adult (e.g. her juvenile sense of humor) and the residents of the house are always referred to as "girls" (not women).

From the evidence of Kaori and Nao, it seems like a wish for a person creates that person in the wisher's world. For whatever reason, Kyoko's wish in the house created Nodoka in Sensei's world. Maybe because that's the world that Kyoko is actually "supposed" to be in, given that her real body is still there - it's only her mind that isn't where it's supposed to be, like a permanent version of one of Sensei's blackouts.

A last thought: there's a good chance that Kyoko's wish was more complex than just wishing for a daughter. Other mysteries around Nodoka could be explained as part of the wish. I'm thinking of things like her ability to "know everything", how she seems to "see" stuff happening in the upside down house, and how she is able to continue her "research" despite the resets. This is pure supposition, but I wonder if Kyoko wished for someone who would (eventually) be able to save her from the upside down house.
That concludes the evidence for this post, but all three parts of this series build on each other. So if you're still skeptical, you might be convinced by what's to come.

For a long while I resisted the conclusion that Nodoka wasn't "real", but not because the evidence was weak. Rather, I thought it was contradictory with another set of evidence: the clues that Nodoka is Sensei's sister (he literally calls her his sister in a dream!). Part of my breakthrough was realizing that Nodoka isn't Sensei's sister, but the hints that she is are more than just red herrings. My theory for what they actually mean is coming in part 2 (which isn't written yet, so it might be a while).
