Simultaneously, she also poses a question “which one am I?” (referring to the idea of there being multiple narrators that Himawari expresses way, way earlier into the game) and follows it up with “perhaps I could show you”, which then *immediately* transitions to an image of Maya standing on the beach under the glow of all three different-colored moons – a very clever instance of foreshadowing in hindsight, considering how this entire event chain ultimately concludes. Now, most of what consequently occurs in the middle: Makoto showing up, inviting Maya to the sleepover party, them both getting unexpectedly interrupted by Ami, etcetera – is, admittedly, not that important or relevant (aside from Ami being depicted with a gigantic red moon behind her, in combination with how the presence of “red” as a whole completely disappears from the event after she leaves), but once two of the girls go away, with only Makoto staying behind, *that’s* when the truly interesting part starts:
The narration resumes – though I’m torn on whether that’s still Himawari or not, because the entire scene carries a strong implication of there now being two conflicting narrators instead of just one, but trying to determine who says what is extremely difficult (with the sole exception of the very final line) – speaking about the “colored lights that must mean something” over an image of Makoto standing under a green moon. The light then suddenly changes from green to blue, as the narrator rejects their previous claim and states that “it’s all just a trick of the camera, a prank on your perception, leading you astray from the words on the screen when all they’ve ever been is honest!”, while also using a cryptic wordplay/metaphor about “the correct/right and the wrong/left hands” (which is curiously similar to what HOPE says to Akira in “I'm Not Here” – *another* Makoto event, same as “A Matter of Time”, now that I think about it). Finally, the actual “climax” of this confrontation is heralded by Yumi’s surprising appearance on the beach, with both narrators taking turns describing basically the same things, until Himawari – having temporarily wrestled back control, and clearly being in a state of high distress – desperately cries out
“Why is it always the beach?! I’m still reeling from the last time, and you expect me to just go on like it’s nothing?! Is *this* the perfect harmony that you hoped for?!”
before being permanently cut off – presumably, by the second narrator she was speaking to – as the colors briefly flicker between green and blue, ultimately settling on blue for the remainder of the event.
In my eyes – based on the aforementioned “color theory” – there are effectively two ways to interpret what happened there. The first (and most likely) way is to chalk it all up to being Pareidolia’s doing, hinted at by the initial prevalence of the color green, deliberate talk of “perception”, Hima getting kicked off right after Yumi – Pareidolia’s current host – enters the scene, and the fact that achieving this nebulous “perfect harmony” appears to primarily be *his* goal, meaning that the entity Himawari blames for the Spring Beach Trip’s conclusion (and the one who cuts her off at the end of “A Matter of Time”) is almost certainly him. The second interpretation, meanwhile, involves a third party – either HOPE or Tenchou, depending on which one do you believe aligns more closely with the color blue – essentially making a power play against Pareidolia (by literally “overriding” his color with their own and then actively denying his perception-centric worldview), with Himawari being more-or-less accidentally caught in the crossfire – her frantic callback to the “perfect harmony” meant as a desperate outcry of someone who decidedly *did not* fucking sign up for this. And if my last claim sounds a bit far-fetched to some of you, do keep in mind that Hima is *the only* other character in the game (aside from mister Concerned himself) to ever directly speak of this “harmony”: in her “torii” narration from the titular event – so there is a very high chance that these two have been (at least partially) working together for a fairly long time, or otherwise align in their personal ambitions to an unexpectedly high degree.
(Full disclosure: I also initially wanted to analyze the ending to “Perfect Harmony” itself – the one with the three moons that appear, each with a different sky, before it cuts away to an image of a torii and the “Please be patient: the end is loading” sequence – but eventually decided against it, as it would require me to go in-depth into the entirely separate “sky” symbology and what all of the different skies are supposed to embody/represent, leading to this section quickly becoming even more bloated and unfocused than it already is. The analysis itself *might* still happen as a separate post sometime later down the line, if I ever feel like it – which, knowing me, I probably will – but not right now, because I would rather not get distracted too much from the main topic at hand.)
Now, while there are still quite a few less prominent color/moon-related mysteries that I would also like to address – like Nao-chan having all three major colors as parts of her visual design (in addition to her own color apparently being “purple”), a second chromatic pattern that is less ubiquitous but still fairly prevalent throughout the entire game (that being “red-green”), or a decent number of relatively obscure early references to the moon or moonlight pertaining to characters such as Yumi, Amiokay or Yasu – I am afraid that this section is already *way* longer than I originally intended it to be, so I’ll limit myself to just one more comparatively major enigma: the cryptic “false moon” message sent by Makoto (or, rather, someone clearly speaking *through* her) following “I Won't Say I'm In Love”.
To quickly get the obvious part out of the way, “when the false moon is upon us” undoubtedly refers to Pareidolia and the advent of his season: we already had explicit confirmation of him not being accepted by the other members of the Trinity (Pareidolia’s dialogue in “A Life of Prizes”), and many of Yasu’s events in Chapter 3 equally deliberately paint him as a clear outsider in HOPE’s and Tenchou’s eternal and “natural” tug of war. As for the identity of the one so transparently manipulating Makoto in this scene, my very confident bet is on HOPE: the flowery but vulgar language used in the text messages doesn’t exactly line up with USER2’s usual calm demeanor, but *does* line up with how USER1 frequently speaks (excluding the caps lock); plus, there is the “egg” connection (“Egg Tooth”, “Somnambula”, Yasu’s tea party in “Down The Rabbit Hole”, etcetera), the fact that HOPE was the only God to ever interact with Sensei through his phone (Uta’s picture, and what happens if you try to delete it), and Nozomu being the guilty party here could also explain both the speaker knowing Akira’s true name and Makoto’s not necessarily uncharacteristic, but still fairly extreme horniness that she displays in the attached photo and the other two possible reply choices. Thus, “one of us” who “is dead now” is most likely USER4, which only really leaves the question of who us this mysterious “she” whom the other three USERs are so desperately trying to “fix” (to then “fix ourselves”). Amiokay? Sekai, perhaps, if we’re going with the “she who is the World Itself” interpretation? Maya, as unlikely as it is? Or someone else entirely?

spoilers.title: “Opening the door”
spoilers.html:
This one, thankfully, is going to be both fairly short and fairly straightforward (no insane 1000 IQ theories, I promise), as the following section is not so much an analysis as it is a simple collection of about a dozen examples, all backing up a single (pretty self-explanatory) thesis. My main (and only) goal here is to just illustrate a certain running theme that some people might not be aware of, because there really isn’t much to “guess” or “speculate” about in relation to this particular subject.

Near the end of Nodoka’s “Hark! Now I Hear Them” 0.54 event, she brings up the symbolic idea of “finding the right door and someone to open it”: a door that apparently leads “somewhere beyond the reach of God” to where Akira will supposedly be able to “find what you are looking for”. In addition to being a semi-reference to something she already told him once (the ending of the aptly-named “Beyond the Reach of God”: “Turn around! Face the door! Open it! And walk in the direction you seldom walk in! This is how we find it! This is how we uncover the truth!”), “opening the door” in itself is a consistent metaphor repeatedly used by various meta-aware characters throughout the entire game to broadly represent rejection of falsehood, enlightenment and/or liberation from the divine control (if not the Wishing Well system itself).

This concept is first mentioned by Amiokay in “The Room with Clocks”, where she tearfully begs Sensei to “Wake up. That’s the key. That’s how we open the door.” right before being kidnapped by Nozomu’s angels – something that is later echoed in “Three Girls in a Line on the Beach” through the line “HOPE is the answer, but won’t be the key!”. Aside from her, the two characters who most frequently reference this theme in their dialogue are Ami and Sekai – though, in a plot twist of the fucking century, they appear to have directly conflicting views on the matter: Ami insistently tries to persuade Akira against opening the door (shown in “Heaven for Human Blood” and “Rain King”, the latter of which even has a second instance of this metaphor with Yuu, Saki and Miu), while Sekai seems to not-so-subtly push him towards it (implied by “Run, Rabbit, Run (Why the Fieldmice Hide)” and *especially* what she says to Akira in “Worry Not, The Mason Jar”).

Moreover, collecting nine keys (or nine pieces of a key) in order to open the door and leave the room you were confined in is the win condition of at least two Reset puzzle events: “A Life of Prizes” and “Times New Roman” – and the latter also features the repeated Voice Over PA messages asserting that “you are happy here” and that “there is no reason for you to leave” (with “Remember to Smile” even framing Maya’s erasure as “punishment” for Sensei going against what the Voice told him). Likewise, “opening the door” (by heeding Gossamer’s advice and then accepting her help) is exactly what Akira does in “Episcopalis: Pickled Plums & Polyrhythmic Psalms”, which in the context of that event symbolizes his resolve to abandon the comfortable dream world of his current comatose state and go back to reality. And, of course, there are *two more* doors that hold an even greater narrative significance: the one on the second floor of Tojo Ramen (apparently leading to “the underlying truth of everything”, which Akira gets very close to opening on multiple occasions, but only actually manages to do it in “WORMGOD54”), as well as the one he and Nao-chan find in the middle of the woods in “Flora” (which results in a direct conflict between USER2, who seemingly put it there and openly urges Sensei to “//////OPEN THE DOOR”, and Pareidolia, who clearly pisses his pants upon seeing this shit go down and panicky orders Akira to absolutely *not* listen to Tenchou under any circumstances).

spoilers.title: Nao-chan
spoilers.html:
Finally, let’s take a moment to briefly talk about Nao-chan and try to accurately sum up everything we know about her, because as much as the girl’s last three or four character events did to greatly humanize her in my eyes and transform lil’ Nao from a walking plot device to an actual person who exists beyond just her meta-role as Akira’s “miracle”, she still is, by all accounts, the most mysterious “human” character among those actually residing in Kumon-mi (meaning Akira and all thirty-five girls with their own face/name cards in the menu), having only extremely vague and scattered hints in regards to her origins, goals and allegiances – which is exactly what I want to address in this section.

First of all, to be totally honest, I’m not sure if I completely buy the “Nao-chan is a wish made by Kaori” theory, because that idea isn’t exactly congruent with the implication of her being an artificial Wishing Well construct of some kind, deliberately sent to Kumon-mi by an unknown third party to facilitate the process of successfully reaching a certain desired outcome (most likely whatever Akira is *actually* supposed to be doing in here, rather than his current MO of endlessly fucking around). I mean, if we *do* assume that Nao-chan is just some weird kid with secret Life-giving powers that Kaori randomly wished for one day (something that I don’t think was ever actually foreshadowed in any substantial way throughout the first two Chapters, because Kaori appeared to be perfectly happy with just John to take care of and – as far as I remember, anyway – never once mentioned wanting to be a mother), then how does it explain her being called “a gift from those who think you need it” by the narrator in “Where the Trees Live”, or the system notifications repeatedly referring to Nao-chan as “TEMPLATE9” on two separate occasions throughout the Camping Trip event chain (while simultaneously confirming her to have a direct affiliation with USER4 in some way, due to the very final line of “What's in the Pot?”), or Pareidolia insisting that his knowledge, albeit much more complete than Sensei’s, is “nowhere near as vast as I want it to be – and that *thing* lies beyond the boundaries of it” (in “Even Gods Get Lost”)?

No, it is my firm belief that the Kaori thing is either an intentional red herring (supported only by a single line of dialogue from “Il Servo”) or something that we don’t currently possess the full necessary context for, and that Nao-chan’s *actual* “biological mother” (insofar as such a concept is even applicable to her) is someone else entirely – someone whose identity has been explicitly foreshadowed as early as the aforementioned “Where the Trees Live”, and was all but spelled out in the girl’s most recent 0.56 character event, “Menma”. In case the obvious name connection didn’t already make it apparent, I am, of course, talking about Nao the Xoanon – the condescending, manipulative, nigh omniscient observer entity tasked with presiding over the Great Library and “cataloguing all that you’ve felt and all that you’ll feel”.

I have very little doubt in my mind that *it* – or, well, *she*, I suppose – was the one who called Nao-chan “a gift” in the event directly preceding the girl’s actual introduction into the story (as the line “I tell you this not as someone recollecting the past, but as someone experiencing the present right there with you” seems to clearly reference Nao’s main role as the chronicler – the one who has “watched it all” – that she uses to describe her own divine purpose during their brief encounter in “Mother’s Milk”), and that it was also the Xoanon who repeatedly referred to Nao-chan as “my daughter” during “Menma”, acting openly protective/possessive towards her (“confront those who seek to reshape you in images other than mine”) and instructing the child to “be more like me” in a very parent-like manner – especially since that both “Menma” and “Mother’s Milk” have a certain underlying thematic parallel: the idea of facing something infinitely beyond your comprehension and being forced to acknowledge just how tiny and insignificant both you and your understanding of the world are when the curtain hiding the truth gets lifted even just a little, before being promptly returned to your “normal life”, as if nothing had ever happened, but with that newfound awareness still lingering somewhere in the back of your head.

And if I wanted to go *even further* into the realm of insane speculation, then I could also link that one line from the ending of “Menma” (following Nao-chan crawling into sleeping Akira’s arms) where the narrator says

“[…] and the fish no longer meant anything to her at all. Nothing did. Just now and Nao, and now Nao and him and Him. Him? Which one do I mean? The placement ruins it all.”

to my other theory of Sensei somehow being USER4, and use this connection to try and take a stab at what Selebus implied “will likely never be explained outside of DLC”. Because a lot of what the Xoanon says in “Mother’s Milk” can arguably be interpreted as one-sided, but still genuine expression of twisted romantic love by an eldritch entity with a very different definition of it (“Every single thing that you’ve felt, I’ve felt as well: each fellatio, ejaculation, penetration, defloration – they’ve all flowed through me! You’ve copulated with *me* more times than with anyone!”), and Nao-chan effectively being their “daughter” – with Nao as the “mother”, and USER4 as the “father” – could likewise potentially explain this borderline instinctual attachment/obligation she feels towards Akira (and also her inherent desire to fuck him, because she is part Arakawa and things like that just run in the family).

How does this proposed theory relate to anything else that happened in “Menma”: the whole “fish” business, the “unfinished butterfly” reference, Sensei dreaming of a lake and Ami interrupting said dream, the significance of the Great Overlook itself and the frog that apparently used to reside there, or Youdidid cryptically saying that “we were the only ones rooting for your success” and “perhaps your world is doomed after all” – I still have no idea (no more than I did when I first played through this event, anyway: you can find my initial thoughts amongst the early discussions of 0.56), aside from the clear implication that Nao-chan is “defective” in some way: her lack of voice turning out to be a bug, not a feature.

Welp, not exactly “later *this* week” (I fucking suck at planning ahead – what else is new?), but better late than never, I suppose, so here it is: the long-awaited (not really) Part 2 of my post covering all of the recent unsolved mysteries in LiL. Without further ado, here we go:

This is something that, admittedly, only occurred to me *after* I already posted Part 1 and decided to indulge my perfectionist paranoia by going through it one more time to hunt for potential typos and such that may have eluded me earlier (so I guess this is just one more benefit to me splitting the original post in two, since I wouldn’t have stumbled upon this realization otherwise), but there is a fairly good chance that the two “planes” that are located above and below Kumon-mi (as per my proposed interpretation) might quite literally be Heaven and Hell.

The primary thing that gives credence to this theory is a certain line of narration said by Himawari in “The Legacy of Thaum (On a Bus)”, where she openly tells Sensei that “Heaven isn’t real – at least not in the way you think” and then follows it up with “Hell, on the other hand, *is* real – but again, not in the way you think”. This ambiguous way of phrasing it that is neither a confirmation nor an open rebuttal strongly implies – to me, anyway – that both “Heaven” and “Hell” *are* actually real physical places (well, under some definition of “real” – the Wishing Well is very wacky when it comes to this kind of stuff), but their nature somehow greatly differs from our implicit universal understanding of how these two realms should be like.

Then, of course, we have the Gods themselves – HOPE and Tenchou, each with their own unique relation to one of the aforementioned planes:

Nozomu’s ties to Heaven are extremely obvious, as he is the one who most unambiguously embodies the traditional idea of Ibrahimic God (a supreme monotheistic deity with angels as servants by his side, who is called “everyone’s Father” and seemingly preaches the general values of humility and self-sacrifice – through the worship ritual of “willingly giving up your eyes” that Yasu discusses in “Sakura Season” – even though these virtues have clearly been twisted into something much more callous), which is then only further compounded by the fact that “belief in Heaven” appears to be something that is deeply inherent to the Arakawa family as a whole: in “Rain King” Ami brings up that “grandma believed in Heaven; mom too, near the end; and you already know my thoughts on the matter from our bus ride backwards”, which can also arguably be extended to Saki (as a fair conjecture based on her general religious baggage). And for an even further proof of this connection, I can confidently point to the “CRITICAL ERROR” sequence from “Memories” with a system message that states “There is no place in Heaven for rapists. There is no place in Heaven for anyone. Maximum capacity has already been reached.” followed directly by “PRAISE THE CALLOUS GOD”, or how HOPE’s resting place is apparently called “Underheaven” according to Yasu in “Miserably Ever After”.

Tenchou’s association with Hell, meanwhile, is a bit more tenuous, but it *is* there (albeit far less obvious): the “Trinity Pt.” Happy Scene related to him being titled “Hell is Empty”, for example, or “Word of the Day” (an event that I already directly connected to Tenchou in Part 1) opening with Sensei’s “affection with GOD being reset to 0” and him “going to Hell”.

So, yeah, this last-minute addition to the theory lines up pretty neatly with the whole “light vs darkness”, “white vs black” duality these two have going on, *and* it could also potentially answer the question I raised earlier, about why Yasu so adamantly insists that there is only *one* other plane of existence aside from Kumon-mi itself: well, because the other-other one is the domain of HOPE’s eternal enemy and thus something that she views as deeply profane, so it isn’t worthy of being acknowledged on the same level as Nozomu’s own sacred realm.

Now, I’m not sure how many people have actually caught this back when the version 0.50 first released (*if* there was anyone who caught it at all: I don’t really remember seeing any discussions about this particular subject when I was reading through the entire thread back in early December, though I suppose I could have simply missed it amongst the sea of other posts), but – and please correct me if I’m wrong on this front – Sara’s “Worthless Me” is *the first* event in the entirety of Lessons in Love that features a first-person narration done by a main POV character who is *not* Sensei.

Because (once again, if I’m not mistaken) literally every single other instance of narration in the entire game unequivocally falls under one of two categories: Akira narrating directly to himself or the commentary being done by some omniscient third party (who may occasionally refer to *themselves* in first person, but never to the people they are narrating about – even when they are clearly one and the same, like in “Soon (Another Nightmare)” and “The Art of Tribadism”: two events very obviously featuring both Ami-the-character and Ami-the-narrator that were nonetheless fully narrated in third person despite that) – yet Sara is the first (and only) one to actively break this pattern (thus far, anyway) for reasons that we can only speculate about. This peculiarity becomes even more noticeable in her next event, “Two for the Price of One”, that begins with Sensei’s first-person narration (like normal) and then seamlessly transitions to Sara’s first-person narration once Akira goes upstairs together with Sana – a subtle switch in perspectives that is equally unprecedented.

There is something else, though – something that’s even more intriguing about Sara. While her allusion to Pegasus and Gossamer in “Worthless Me” is extremely obvious and generally hard to miss, what’s far *less* obvious is that throughout that entire event Sara is not just internally narrating to herself, but rather one-sidedly communicating with that very same abstract and mysterious observer entity that Akira occasionally references in his monologues, strongly implied by the lines “You probably think I’m crazy, don’t you – always telling you things like this” and “If you were real, would you hold me? Just me? Or is there no world in the trillions that exist where I, alone, am enough?”. What’s more, her choice of words and general demeanor also make it clear that this is not just a random one-off occurrence, but something that she has been doing for a very long time: living her whole life (or at least the majority of it, from teenage years onwards) always being aware that there is someone, somewhere observing your every feeling, thought and action and getting into a habit of instinctively talking to that vague presence (just like Akira constantly does) without ever actually hoping to get a response or even knowing who she is talking *to*.

All of this makes me confident in my assumption that there is *another* layer of connection between Sara and Akira that goes much deeper than just what was revealed to us in “The Creaking of the Seventh Step” and “Halfway Down the Wishing Well”, and that all of their other shared similarities, like occasionally experiencing “blackouts” or being inexorably sought after by the divine, are not unrelated self-contained traits, but rather symptoms – manifestations of the same underlying root cause.

This segment is probably going to be way less substantial than the others, because there is just inherently very little info to go off – definitely not enough to build a working theory that doesn’t immediately cross into heavy speculation territory – but I still decided to include it for informative purposes, if nothing else.

It is a well-established fact – both in narrative and in gameplay – that time is effectively meaningless in Kumon-mi. The day count is basically just for show and stops being anywhere near close to even remotely resembling reality halfway through Chapter 2 (if not earlier), the holidays and other important days aggressively blend together into one indistinguishable mess (sometimes literally – fuck you, Christmasloween) with zero regard to what month is actually written on the calendar, and LiL’s deliberate avoidance of any and all mentions of the exact ages of the canonically underage characters in the increasingly stupider and blatantly artificial ways has long since turned from a meta plot point into a hilarious running joke.

So with all of the constant Resets, missing seasons of the year and other temporal bullshit going on, it’s not at all a surprise that the game is *extremely* stingy with giving us *any* concrete dates, to the point where prior to the version 0.52 we only really had two of them that were ever directly stated within the text: “December 28th, 2020”, which is the date of the fifth Reset slumber party (that then leads into “Untitled”), the reoccurring date on all of Nodoka’s notes (that she brings up in “Mille Crepe” as proof that “we’re all just actors blindly repeating the same play over and over again”), and also Himawari’s birthday, I believe (though I genuinely have no idea where this last claim originates from, as I couldn’t find a source for it *anywhere* in my notes, but still vividly remember it being mentioned somewhere), and “August 31st, 2030”, which is listed on an old semi-hidden calendar in “Times New Roman” (giving us at least a rough estimate of how long it’s been between “present” times and whenever “Times New Roman” takes place, and… not really serving any other purpose aside from that, from my personal understanding).

However, the sixth Beach update (both parts of it: 0.52 and 0.53) has also added *two more* dates into the mix: “January 1st, 2020” and “January 1st, 2036” – which are curiously and *very coincidentally* exactly sixteen years apart. The first one shows up in “Spam”, sourced from what seems to be someone’s death certificate – presumably one belonging to a newborn child, judging by four distorted images of infants immediately preceding the date itself (these infants are also for some reason displayed over an image of “catacombs” from the Great Pareidolia Mall – a location that contains the only known exit from the Mall and whose binary index “01110100” directly corresponds to the letter “T” – with an equally weird text-to-speech mentioning “her”). The second one, meanwhile, appears on the final title card in “Like Lions” (notable for being the only of the three title cards with an actual date, rather than something vague like “2 months later, October”), which is the event where Himawari’s paradise gets derailed twice: first by the sudden call from Ami, and then by “real” Himawari herself.

So what is the significance of these dates? Well, considering that two – or potentially three, if that claim that I cannot find the source of is indeed correct – of them seem to be directly related to our happy little sunflower (in fact, the entire sixth Beach event chain is quite unambiguously connected to her, for self-explanatory reasons), I think that it’s exceedingly clear what – or, rather, *who* – should be our main starting point if we want to make an attempt of trying to get to the bottom of this, even if it means accepting the predominantly speculative nature of the whole process.

(Which, unfortunately, also means that I am a fucking liar, because I explicitly promised that that none of the mysteries in this post will in any way involve Himawari. Whoops… Oh well.)

Now, ignoring the year for a second and looking at just the first part of the dates, “December 28th" as the date of birth followed by “January 1st” as the date of death line up pretty neatly with the “death certificate for an infant” interpretation, since the child would have been less than a weak old at that point. The year part, of course, doesn’t make sense, since both dates read “2020”, which following the normal chronological order would necessarily imply that the owner of that death certificate, whoever it is, died almost twelve whole months before Himawari was born, naturally excluding her from the list of potential suspects – except, well, the Wishing Well is a timey-wimey magic bullshit land where it can be any year you want for as long as you want, and so the “same year” discrepancy does not necessarily disprove shit.

Furthermore, there have been at least two Happy Scenes actively featuring newborn Himawari, in one of which Akira is shown to be severely struggling with raising her alone (“Arms Bent Back”), while in the other she is miraculously saved by Ayane from a situation that would otherwise almost certainly lead to her being injured, if not worse (“Sally Sells Seashells”). And that is without bringing up the still-unexplained Unnamed Baby from “Trinity Pt. III: Non Est Deus” (who, just to remind everyone, was canonically stillborn), or the reality of Ayane unwillingly getting the quickest abortion in Kumon-mi thanks to the Reset shenanigans – and, obviously, there is *no chance in hell* that the exact sixteen-year difference between the date of death on the certificate and Aomori-Himawari’s metaphorical “death” is *just* a happy coincidence. Point is, provided that even a few of these narrative connections are actually correct and not just a product of my overly active imagination, there appears to be a decently strong thematic implication of Himawari either experiencing a very difficult early childhood or suffering some unfortunate (and likely lethal) complication during birth/in her infancy.

And if I *really* wanted to go full schizo, then I could *also* cite that one relatively obscure “current Ami is the result of a wish made by Sekai” theory that dates back to somewhere around 0.45 (with the wish itself in this case being to drastically alter the course of events and allow Ami – the child Sekai was already physically pregnant with at the time – to be born safely, rather than dying in the womb like she was originally supposed to) and directly apply it to Ayane without even really having to change anything:

Under this new deranged conjecture of mine, the original Himawari died less than a week after her birth, which then caused the original Ayane – who, understandably, was beyond herself with grief – to wish for a world where this never happened. Thus, the Himawari we know instead comes from *that* secondary reality: a reality where she was born healthy and lived a relatively normal, happy life together with her parents – which importantly doesn’t contradict Himawari’s own claim that she is “[Akira’s] real, blood-related future daughter” from “Aomori”, because the exact mechanics at play here are notably different between the specifics of how Maya came into existence (and this Hima wouldn’t know shit about what happened in the so-called “original” world anyway). In fact, I could even point to Ayane asking “Have I used mine yet?” (referring to the singular allotted wish per human) in “Last Supper” as a clear foreshadowing for this exact future plot point, when in a cruel twist of dramatic irony it is later going to be revealed that Himawari’s goal of returning Ayane and Akira to “where they are truly supposed to be” means that she won’t *actually* be able to reunite with them there, because *that world’s* Hima has been dead for God knows how long, while *this* Hima fundamentally originates from a completely separate version of reality and thus cannot follow suit with her parents no matter how much she wants to.

Or maybe I’m just totally wrong on all fronts, and none of this is *even remotely* close to the truth. Stay tuned to find out, I guess.

Now, the thing that gave me the push to finally take a stab at this particular area of analysis – something that I wanted to do for a very long time, but somehow never really got a proper drive to – was re-reading A Matter of Time” (an event that we’ll discuss in much more detail relatively shortly) for the second time during my most recent replay of the game and then going back to double-check all of the previous events also featuring the three titular moons, in a vain hope to potentially try and find some consistent element between all of their appearances, which would in turn hopefully allow me do determine which RGB color corresponds to which God. And, shockingly, I actually *did* find what I was looking for. Because, as it turns out, even though most of the time the moons just appear neutrally-white, without any discernable size or color differences between them, the two notable exceptions where they *are* deliberately distinguished through color – “Cicadian Rhythm (The Gardener)” and “A Matter of Time” – unexpectedly both feature them in the same consistent pattern: red, blue, green.

To be honest, my first reaction to this discovery was not one of happiness, but rather one of reasonable skepticism. I understood that what I just found could barely be called “proof” at all and had all intention to just Occam’s Razor it away as a simple coincidence, arguing that “red-blue-green” is nothing but a visually striking color gradient Selebus has a particular affinity for (because this exact pattern *does* frequently show up in many other events throughout the game, like “The Virgin of the Apocalypse” or “God of Light”, without being explicitly tied to the moons themselves), and so it was probably just accidentally copy-pasted in a way that creates an illusion of meaning – where, in actuality, there is none. However, after sitting on that initial skeptical assumption for a little while, I ultimately dismissed it as rationally improbable, because while the “accidental color gradient” argument could *maybe* work for “A Matter of Time”, the way the moons were depicted in “Cicadian Rhythm (The Gardener)” was *way* too deliberate for it to just be an unintentional byproduct of a generic color filter. And once *that* conviction took root, my thoughts then immediately went to the semi-final image of “All That’s Left Are Stars”, wondering “well, how does this red-blue-green pattern that I discovered line up with the order in which the Gods’ faces were shown there?”.

Out of all members of the Trinity, the easiest one to match is definitely Pareidolia, as the third face in “All That’s Left Are Stars” undoubtedly belongs to him *and* there is already a decent number of hints connecting him to the color green, like the gigantic green moon behind Akira in “The Collector” or how in “Run, Rabbit, Run (Why the Fieldmice Hide)” – Kaori’s final event of Chapter 3 – she mentions her main fear being “the color green”, yet in “Tree Village (The Color Machine)” – her very next character event, and the first one of Chapter 4 – she has now completely changed her tune and confidently states that “my outside color is green”.

Matching the other two Gods, however, is… a little complicated, mostly due to a whole mountain of scattered and directly conflicting proof. Because while the simplest and most intuitive interpretation is to assume that the first frowning face is Tenchou (because he *has* been depicted as frowning a couple of times) and that the second smiling face is HOPE (because Nozomu is always portrayed as smiling), making the color designation be “Tenchou/Red” and “HOPE/Blue”, there *is* a way (mostly utilizing severe mental gymnastics) to instead read it as Nozomu being the frowning one (since his “face” is always upside-down, making it look like a frown) – and thus red – and Tenchou being the smiling one (because he is always “calm”) – and thus blue. Each version has its own separate heap of evidence backing it up, so for the sake of fairness and objectivity I will be arguing in favor of both of them, in order to not accidentally fall victim to my own confirmation bias.

For the “Tenchou is Red, HOPE is blue” theory, we have “red weather” from “Trinity Pt. II: Hell is Empty” (though this can also be argued to instead signify HOPE, since the event itself mostly focuses on him and his angels rather than Tenchou), Sensei “feeling callous tonight” and choosing “blue” as his favorite color in “Bluejay” (kind of the only thing linking HOPE to blue, really), red prominently being featured during a certain creepy interaction with USER2 in “Backwards Dancing”, Tojo Ramen having red emergency lights that activate during the blackouts caused by Tenchou’s life-support machinery (might just be a perfectly normal thing, but, hey, you never know), Yasu’s adamant insistence that “red is bad” (introduced in “Sore Thumb” and then reaffirmed in “Etinsib Ziwa and The Book of Colors”), and also the whole thing with the Red Room in “Arms Bent Back” (which I am aware is a Twin Peaks reference, but the event itself is also strongly connected to Tenchou, so…).

On the other hand, “HOPE is red, Tenchou is blue” interpretation is supported by HOPE’s own red smile – his signature and most defining visual element – in addition to red just in general being very heavily associated with the Arakawas (Sekai’s/Ami’s eyes and hair, teenager Akira hurting his hand at school to the point of major bleeding and then having Sekai take care of that wound being one of his core memories of her, etcetera), the discussion about how “some people consider red to be an evil color, even though it can be rather beautiful under certain circumstances” from “The Color of a Heart” (which is Yasu’s first “proper” introduction into the story after her brief initial appearance in Sana’s “The Girl in the Black Dress”), Youdidid and Moyo (who explicitly work for HOPE) frequently being seen wearing a red dress and also guarding the Orb of Red in “SENSEI-QUEST”, and Yasu possessing the Red Key in “Times New Roman” (a key that opens the Locker/Book №7 containing a bright green eraser). As for how Tenchou is connected to the color blue… well, the only potential argument that I can come up with is simply by proxy of his *other* thematic tie: the one to the ocean (which is… blue and stuff) – though just that on its own is understandably very weak and can barely constitute as “proof” even in my eyes.

Still, now that we (at least arguably) have a working theory of assigning colors to Gods and theoretically discerning who is who, let’s go back to “A Matter of Time” – an event that *greatly* intrigued me both times I played through it, yet hasn’t really been discussed in this thread at all for whatever reason, from what I remember – and try to understand what exactly was happening there:

“A Matter of Time” opens with Himawari – and it is *very* obviously her, judging by how she explicitly mentions “settling down somewhere up north, maybe in Aomori” and then claims to “always be there for you, because you’ll always be looking for me” (with an even more telling “I would not exist at all if it was not for your unending love” line) – reiterating the idea that “it won’t last forever” and that “time is running out, but I still believe that you are here for a reason”. Simultaneously, she also poses a question “which one am I?” (referring to the idea of there being multiple narrators that Himawari expresses way, way earlier into the game) and follows it up with “perhaps I could show you”, which then *immediately* transitions to an image of Maya standing on the beach under the glow of all three different-colored moons – a very clever instance of foreshadowing in hindsight, considering how this entire event chain ultimately concludes. Now, most of what consequently occurs in the middle: Makoto showing up, inviting Maya to the sleepover party, them both getting unexpectedly interrupted by Ami, etcetera – is, admittedly, not that important or relevant (aside from Ami being depicted with a gigantic red moon behind her, in combination with how the presence of “red” as a whole completely disappears from the event after she leaves), but once two of the girls go away, with only Makoto staying behind, *that’s* when the truly interesting part starts:

The narration resumes – though I’m torn on whether that’s still Himawari or not, because the entire scene carries a strong implication of there now being two conflicting narrators instead of just one, but trying to determine who says what is extremely difficult (with the sole exception of the very final line) – speaking about the “colored lights that must mean something” over an image of Makoto standing under a green moon. The light then suddenly changes from green to blue, as the narrator rejects their previous claim and states that “it’s all just a trick of the camera, a prank on your perception, leading you astray from the words on the screen when all they’ve ever been is honest!”, while also using a cryptic wordplay/metaphor about “the correct/right and the wrong/left hands” (which is curiously similar to what HOPE says to Akira in “I'm Not Here” – *another* Makoto event, same as “A Matter of Time”, now that I think about it). Finally, the actual “climax” of this confrontation is heralded by Yumi’s surprising appearance on the beach, with both narrators taking turns describing basically the same things, until Himawari – having temporarily wrestled back control, and clearly being in a state of high distress – desperately cries out

“Why is it always the beach?! I’m still reeling from the last time, and you expect me to just go on like it’s nothing?! Is *this* the perfect harmony that you hoped for?!”

before being permanently cut off – presumably, by the second narrator she was speaking to – as the colors briefly flicker between green and blue, ultimately settling on blue for the remainder of the event.

In my eyes – based on the aforementioned “color theory” – there are effectively two ways to interpret what happened there. The first (and most likely) way is to chalk it all up to being Pareidolia’s doing, hinted at by the initial prevalence of the color green, deliberate talk of “perception”, Hima getting kicked off right after Yumi – Pareidolia’s current host – enters the scene, and the fact that achieving this nebulous “perfect harmony” appears to primarily be *his* goal, meaning that the entity Himawari blames for the Spring Beach Trip’s conclusion (and the one who cuts her off at the end of “A Matter of Time”) is almost certainly him. The second interpretation, meanwhile, involves a third party – either HOPE or Tenchou, depending on which one do you believe aligns more closely with the color blue – essentially making a power play against Pareidolia (by literally “overriding” his color with their own and then actively denying his perception-centric worldview), with Himawari being more-or-less accidentally caught in the crossfire – her frantic callback to the “perfect harmony” meant as a desperate outcry of someone who decidedly *did not* fucking sign up for this. And if my last claim sounds a bit far-fetched to some of you, do keep in mind that Hima is *the only* other character in the game (aside from mister Concerned himself) to ever directly speak of this “harmony”: in her “torii” narration from the titular event – so there is a very high chance that these two have been (at least partially) working together for a fairly long time, or otherwise align in their personal ambitions to an unexpectedly high degree.

(Full disclosure: I also initially wanted to analyze the ending to “Perfect Harmony” itself – the one with the three moons that appear, each with a different sky, before it cuts away to an image of a torii and the “Please be patient: the end is loading” sequence – but eventually decided against it, as it would require me to go in-depth into the entirely separate “sky” symbology and what all of the different skies are supposed to embody/represent, leading to this section quickly becoming even more bloated and unfocused than it already is. The analysis itself *might* still happen as a separate post sometime later down the line, if I ever feel like it – which, knowing me, I probably will – but not right now, because I would rather not get distracted too much from the main topic at hand.)

Now, while there are still quite a few less prominent color/moon-related mysteries that I would also like to address – like Nao-chan having all three major colors as parts of her visual design (in addition to her own color apparently being “purple”), a second chromatic pattern that is less ubiquitous but still fairly prevalent throughout the entire game (that being “red-green”), or a decent number of relatively obscure early references to the moon or moonlight pertaining to characters such as Yumi, Amiokay or Yasu – I am afraid that this section is already *way* longer than I originally intended it to be, so I’ll limit myself to just one more comparatively major enigma: the cryptic “false moon” message sent by Makoto (or, rather, someone clearly speaking *through* her) following “I Won't Say I'm In Love”.

To quickly get the obvious part out of the way, “when the false moon is upon us” undoubtedly refers to Pareidolia and the advent of his season: we already had explicit confirmation of him not being accepted by the other members of the Trinity (Pareidolia’s dialogue in “A Life of Prizes”), and many of Yasu’s events in Chapter 3 equally deliberately paint him as a clear outsider in HOPE’s and Tenchou’s eternal and “natural” tug of war. As for the identity of the one so transparently manipulating Makoto in this scene, my very confident bet is on HOPE: the flowery but vulgar language used in the text messages doesn’t exactly line up with USER2’s usual calm demeanor, but *does* line up with how USER1 frequently speaks (excluding the caps lock); plus, there is the “egg” connection (“Egg Tooth”, “Somnambula”, Yasu’s tea party in “Down The Rabbit Hole”, etcetera), the fact that HOPE was the only God to ever interact with Sensei through his phone (Uta’s picture, and what happens if you try to delete it), and Nozomu being the guilty party here could also explain both the speaker knowing Akira’s true name and Makoto’s not necessarily uncharacteristic, but still fairly extreme horniness that she displays in the attached photo and the other two possible reply choices. Thus, “one of us” who “is dead now” is most likely USER4, which only really leaves the question of who us this mysterious “she” whom the other three USERs are so desperately trying to “fix” (to then “fix ourselves”). Amiokay? Sekai, perhaps, if we’re going with the “she who is the World Itself” interpretation? Maya, as unlikely as it is? Or someone else entirely?

This one, thankfully, is going to be both fairly short and fairly straightforward (no insane 1000 IQ theories, I promise), as the following section is not so much an analysis as it is a simple collection of about a dozen examples, all backing up a single (pretty self-explanatory) thesis. My main (and only) goal here is to just illustrate a certain running theme that some people might not be aware of, because there really isn’t much to “guess” or “speculate” about in relation to this particular subject.

Near the end of Nodoka’s “Hark! Now I Hear Them” 0.54 event, she brings up the symbolic idea of “finding the right door and someone to open it”: a door that apparently leads “somewhere beyond the reach of God” to where Akira will supposedly be able to “find what you are looking for”. In addition to being a semi-reference to something she already told him once (the ending of the aptly-named “Beyond the Reach of God”: “Turn around! Face the door! Open it! And walk in the direction you seldom walk in! This is how we find it! This is how we uncover the truth!”), “opening the door” in itself is a consistent metaphor repeatedly used by various meta-aware characters throughout the entire game to broadly represent rejection of falsehood, enlightenment and/or liberation from the divine control (if not the Wishing Well system itself).

This concept is first mentioned by Amiokay in “The Room with Clocks”, where she tearfully begs Sensei to “Wake up. That’s the key. That’s how we open the door.” right before being kidnapped by Nozomu’s angels – something that is later echoed in “Three Girls in a Line on the Beach” through the line “HOPE is the answer, but won’t be the key!”. Aside from her, the two characters who most frequently reference this theme in their dialogue are Ami and Sekai – though, in a plot twist of the fucking century, they appear to have directly conflicting views on the matter: Ami insistently tries to persuade Akira against opening the door (shown in “Heaven for Human Blood” and “Rain King”, the latter of which even has a second instance of this metaphor with Yuu, Saki and Miu), while Sekai seems to not-so-subtly push him towards it (implied by “Run, Rabbit, Run (Why the Fieldmice Hide)” and *especially* what she says to Akira in “Worry Not, The Mason Jar”).

Moreover, collecting nine keys (or nine pieces of a key) in order to open the door and leave the room you were confined in is the win condition of at least two Reset puzzle events: “A Life of Prizes” and “Times New Roman” – and the latter also features the repeated Voice Over PA messages asserting that “you are happy here” and that “there is no reason for you to leave” (with “Remember to Smile” even framing Maya’s erasure as “punishment” for Sensei going against what the Voice told him). Likewise, “opening the door” (by heeding Gossamer’s advice and then accepting her help) is exactly what Akira does in “Episcopalis: Pickled Plums & Polyrhythmic Psalms”, which in the context of that event symbolizes his resolve to abandon the comfortable dream world of his current comatose state and go back to reality. And, of course, there are *two more* doors that hold an even greater narrative significance: the one on the second floor of Tojo Ramen (apparently leading to “the underlying truth of everything”, which Akira gets very close to opening on multiple occasions, but only actually manages to do it in “WORMGOD54”), as well as the one he and Nao-chan find in the middle of the woods in “Flora” (which results in a direct conflict between USER2, who seemingly put it there and openly urges Sensei to “//////OPEN THE DOOR”, and Pareidolia, who clearly pisses his pants upon seeing this shit go down and panicky orders Akira to absolutely *not* listen to Tenchou under any circumstances).

Finally, let’s take a moment to briefly talk about Nao-chan and try to accurately sum up everything we know about her, because as much as the girl’s last three or four character events did to greatly humanize her in my eyes and transform lil’ Nao from a walking plot device to an actual person who exists beyond just her meta-role as Akira’s “miracle”, she still is, by all accounts, the most mysterious “human” character among those actually residing in Kumon-mi (meaning Akira and all thirty-five girls with their own face/name cards in the menu), having only extremely vague and scattered hints in regards to her origins, goals and allegiances – which is exactly what I want to address in this section.

First of all, to be totally honest, I’m not sure if I completely buy the “Nao-chan is a wish made by Kaori” theory, because that idea isn’t exactly congruent with the implication of her being an artificial Wishing Well construct of some kind, deliberately sent to Kumon-mi by an unknown third party to facilitate the process of successfully reaching a certain desired outcome (most likely whatever Akira is *actually* supposed to be doing in here, rather than his current MO of endlessly fucking around). I mean, if we *do* assume that Nao-chan is just some weird kid with secret Life-giving powers that Kaori randomly wished for one day (something that I don’t think was ever actually foreshadowed in any substantial way throughout the first two Chapters, because Kaori appeared to be perfectly happy with just John to take care of and – as far as I remember, anyway – never once mentioned wanting to be a mother), then how does it explain her being called “a gift from those who think you need it” by the narrator in “Where the Trees Live”, or the system notifications repeatedly referring to Nao-chan as “TEMPLATE9” on two separate occasions throughout the Camping Trip event chain (while simultaneously confirming her to have a direct affiliation with USER4 in some way, due to the very final line of “What's in the Pot?”), or Pareidolia insisting that his knowledge, albeit much more complete than Sensei’s, is “nowhere near as vast as I want it to be – and that *thing* lies beyond the boundaries of it” (in “Even Gods Get Lost”)?

No, it is my firm belief that the Kaori thing is either an intentional red herring (supported only by a single line of dialogue from “Il Servo”) or something that we don’t currently possess the full necessary context for, and that Nao-chan’s *actual* “biological mother” (insofar as such a concept is even applicable to her) is someone else entirely – someone whose identity has been explicitly foreshadowed as early as the aforementioned “Where the Trees Live”, and was all but spelled out in the girl’s most recent 0.56 character event, “Menma”. In case the obvious name connection didn’t already make it apparent, I am, of course, talking about Nao the Xoanon – the condescending, manipulative, nigh omniscient observer entity tasked with presiding over the Great Library and “cataloguing all that you’ve felt and all that you’ll feel”.

I have very little doubt in my mind that *it* – or, well, *she*, I suppose – was the one who called Nao-chan “a gift” in the event directly preceding the girl’s actual introduction into the story (as the line “I tell you this not as someone recollecting the past, but as someone experiencing the present right there with you” seems to clearly reference Nao’s main role as the chronicler – the one who has “watched it all” – that she uses to describe her own divine purpose during their brief encounter in “Mother’s Milk”), and that it was also the Xoanon who repeatedly referred to Nao-chan as “my daughter” during “Menma”, acting openly protective/possessive towards her (“confront those who seek to reshape you in images other than mine”) and instructing the child to “be more like me” in a very parent-like manner – especially since that both “Menma” and “Mother’s Milk” have a certain underlying thematic parallel: the idea of facing something infinitely beyond your comprehension and being forced to acknowledge just how tiny and insignificant both you and your understanding of the world are when the curtain hiding the truth gets lifted even just a little, before being promptly returned to your “normal life”, as if nothing had ever happened, but with that newfound awareness still lingering somewhere in the back of your head.

And if I wanted to go *even further* into the realm of insane speculation, then I could also link that one line from the ending of “Menma” (following Nao-chan crawling into sleeping Akira’s arms) where the narrator says

“[…] and the fish no longer meant anything to her at all. Nothing did. Just now and Nao, and now Nao and him and Him. Him? Which one do I mean? The placement ruins it all.”

to my other theory of Sensei somehow being USER4, and use this connection to try and take a stab at what Selebus implied “will likely never be explained outside of DLC”. Because a lot of what the Xoanon says in “Mother’s Milk” can arguably be interpreted as one-sided, but still genuine expression of twisted romantic love by an eldritch entity with a very different definition of it (“Every single thing that you’ve felt, I’ve felt as well: each fellatio, ejaculation, penetration, defloration – they’ve all flowed through me! You’ve copulated with *me* more times than with anyone!”), and Nao-chan effectively being their “daughter” – with Nao as the “mother”, and USER4 as the “father” – could likewise potentially explain this borderline instinctual attachment/obligation she feels towards Akira (and also her inherent desire to fuck him, because she is part Arakawa and things like that just run in the family).

How does this proposed theory relate to anything else that happened in “Menma”: the whole “fish” business, the “unfinished butterfly” reference, Sensei dreaming of a lake and Ami interrupting said dream, the significance of the Great Overlook itself and the frog that apparently used to reside there, or Youdidid cryptically saying that “we were the only ones rooting for your success” and “perhaps your world is doomed after all” – I still have no idea (no more than I did when I first played through this event, anyway: you can find my initial thoughts amongst the early discussions of 0.56), aside from the clear implication that Nao-chan is “defective” in some way: her lack of voice turning out to be a bug, not a feature.

And now, if I may, I would like to conclude this *titanic* undertaking that took a few arduous weeks to complete with a certain quote from one of my favorite non-LiL characters that I feel would be most appropriate here:

“Simply by the existence of my ascended autism (and two thousand pages of meticulously written notes), this level of reasoning was possible for Charlotte Wiltshire. What do you think, everyone?”

CharlotteWiltshire26 said:
Welp, not exactly “later *this* week” (I fucking suck at planning ahead – what else is new?), but better late than never, I suppose, so here it is: the long-awaited (not really) Part 2 of my post covering all of the recent unsolved mysteries in LiL. Without further ado, here we go:
Spoiler:
An addendum to my previous “Sinkhole” section
This is something that, admittedly, only occurred to me *after* I already posted Part 1 and decided to indulge my perfectionist paranoia by going through it one more time to hunt for potential typos and such that may have eluded me earlier (so I guess this is just one more benefit to me splitting the original post in two, since I wouldn’t have stumbled upon this realization otherwise), but there is a fairly good chance that the two “planes” that are located above and below Kumon-mi (as per my proposed interpretation) might quite literally be Heaven and Hell.
The primary thing that gives credence to this theory is a certain line of narration said by Himawari in “The Legacy of Thaum (On a Bus)”, where she openly tells Sensei that “Heaven isn’t real – at least not in the way you think” and then follows it up with “Hell, on the other hand, *is* real – but again, not in the way you think”. This ambiguous way of phrasing it that is neither a confirmation nor an open rebuttal strongly implies – to me, anyway – that both “Heaven” and “Hell” *are* actually real physical places (well, under some definition of “real” – the Wishing Well is very wacky when it comes to this kind of stuff), but their nature somehow greatly differs from our implicit universal understanding of how these two realms should be like.
Then, of course, we have the Gods themselves – HOPE and Tenchou, each with their own unique relation to one of the aforementioned planes:
Nozomu’s ties to Heaven are extremely obvious, as he is the one who most unambiguously embodies the traditional idea of Ibrahimic God (a supreme monotheistic deity with angels as servants by his side, who is called “everyone’s Father” and seemingly preaches the general values of humility and self-sacrifice – through the worship ritual of “willingly giving up your eyes” that Yasu discusses in “Sakura Season” – even though these virtues have clearly been twisted into something much more callous), which is then only further compounded by the fact that “belief in Heaven” appears to be something that is deeply inherent to the Arakawa family as a whole: in “Rain King” Ami brings up that “grandma believed in Heaven; mom too, near the end; and you already know my thoughts on the matter from our bus ride backwards”, which can also arguably be extended to Saki (as a fair conjecture based on her general religious baggage). And for an even further proof of this connection, I can confidently point to the “CRITICAL ERROR” sequence from “Memories” with a system message that states “There is no place in Heaven for rapists. There is no place in Heaven for anyone. Maximum capacity has already been reached.” followed directly by “PRAISE THE CALLOUS GOD”, or how HOPE’s resting place is apparently called “Underheaven” according to Yasu in “Miserably Ever After”.
Tenchou’s association with Hell, meanwhile, is a bit more tenuous, but it *is* there (albeit far less obvious): the “Trinity Pt.” Happy Scene related to him being titled “Hell is Empty”, for example, or “Word of the Day” (an event that I already directly connected to Tenchou in Part 1) opening with Sensei’s “affection with GOD being reset to 0” and him “going to Hell”.
So, yeah, this last-minute addition to the theory lines up pretty neatly with the whole “light vs darkness”, “white vs black” duality these two have going on, *and* it could also potentially answer the question I raised earlier, about why Yasu so adamantly insists that there is only *one* other plane of existence aside from Kumon-mi itself: well, because the other-other one is the domain of HOPE’s eternal enemy and thus something that she views as deeply profane, so it isn’t worthy of being acknowledged on the same level as Nozomu’s own sacred realm.
Spoiler:
Sara
Now, I’m not sure how many people have actually caught this back when the version 0.50 first released (*if* there was anyone who caught it at all: I don’t really remember seeing any discussions about this particular subject when I was reading through the entire thread back in early December, though I suppose I could have simply missed it amongst the sea of other posts), but – and please correct me if I’m wrong on this front – Sara’s “Worthless Me” is *the first* event in the entirety of Lessons in Love that features a first-person narration done by a main POV character who is *not* Sensei.
Because (once again, if I’m not mistaken) literally every single other instance of narration in the entire game unequivocally falls under one of two categories: Akira narrating directly to himself or the commentary being done by some omniscient third party (who may occasionally refer to *themselves* in first person, but never to the people they are narrating about – even when they are clearly one and the same, like in “Soon (Another Nightmare)” and “The Art of Tribadism”: two events very obviously featuring both Ami-the-character and Ami-the-narrator that were nonetheless fully narrated in third person despite that) – yet Sara is the first (and only) one to actively break this pattern (thus far, anyway) for reasons that we can only speculate about. This peculiarity becomes even more noticeable in her next event, “Two for the Price of One”, that begins with Sensei’s first-person narration (like normal) and then seamlessly transitions to Sara’s first-person narration once Akira goes upstairs together with Sana – a subtle switch in perspectives that is equally unprecedented.
There is something else, though – something that’s even more intriguing about Sara. While her allusion to Pegasus and Gossamer in “Worthless Me” is extremely obvious and generally hard to miss, what’s far *less* obvious is that throughout that entire event Sara is not just internally narrating to herself, but rather one-sidedly communicating with that very same abstract and mysterious observer entity that Akira occasionally references in his monologues, strongly implied by the lines “You probably think I’m crazy, don’t you – always telling you things like this” and “If you were real, would you hold me? Just me? Or is there no world in the trillions that exist where I, alone, am enough?”. What’s more, her choice of words and general demeanor also make it clear that this is not just a random one-off occurrence, but something that she has been doing for a very long time: living her whole life (or at least the majority of it, from teenage years onwards) always being aware that there is someone, somewhere observing your every feeling, thought and action and getting into a habit of instinctively talking to that vague presence (just like Akira constantly does) without ever actually hoping to get a response or even knowing who she is talking *to*.
All of this makes me confident in my assumption that there is *another* layer of connection between Sara and Akira that goes much deeper than just what was revealed to us in “The Creaking of the Seventh Step” and “Halfway Down the Wishing Well”, and that all of their other shared similarities, like occasionally experiencing “blackouts” or being inexorably sought after by the divine, are not unrelated self-contained traits, but rather symptoms – manifestations of the same underlying root cause.
Spoiler:
Dates
This segment is probably going to be way less substantial than the others, because there is just inherently very little info to go off – definitely not enough to build a working theory that doesn’t immediately cross into heavy speculation territory – but I still decided to include it for informative purposes, if nothing else.
It is a well-established fact – both in narrative and in gameplay – that time is effectively meaningless in Kumon-mi. The day count is basically just for show and stops being anywhere near close to even remotely resembling reality halfway through Chapter 2 (if not earlier), the holidays and other important days aggressively blend together into one indistinguishable mess (sometimes literally – fuck you, Christmasloween) with zero regard to what month is actually written on the calendar, and LiL’s deliberate avoidance of any and all mentions of the exact ages of the canonically underage characters in the increasingly stupider and blatantly artificial ways has long since turned from a meta plot point into a hilarious running joke.
So with all of the constant Resets, missing seasons of the year and other temporal bullshit going on, it’s not at all a surprise that the game is *extremely* stingy with giving us *any* concrete dates, to the point where prior to the version 0.52 we only really had two of them that were ever directly stated within the text: “December 28th, 2020”, which is the date of the fifth Reset slumber party (that then leads into “Untitled”), the reoccurring date on all of Nodoka’s notes (that she brings up in “Mille Crepe” as proof that “we’re all just actors blindly repeating the same play over and over again”), and also Himawari’s birthday, I believe (though I genuinely have no idea where this last claim originates from, as I couldn’t find a source for it *anywhere* in my notes, but still vividly remember it being mentioned somewhere), and “August 31st, 2030”, which is listed on an old semi-hidden calendar in “Times New Roman” (giving us at least a rough estimate of how long it’s been between “present” times and whenever “Times New Roman” takes place, and… not really serving any other purpose aside from that, from my personal understanding).
However, the sixth Beach update (both parts of it: 0.52 and 0.53) has also added *two more* dates into the mix: “January 1st, 2020” and “January 1st, 2036” – which are curiously and *very coincidentally* exactly sixteen years apart. The first one shows up in “Spam”, sourced from what seems to be someone’s death certificate – presumably one belonging to a newborn child, judging by four distorted images of infants immediately preceding the date itself (these infants are also for some reason displayed over an image of “catacombs” from the Great Pareidolia Mall – a location that contains the only known exit from the Mall and whose binary index “01110100” directly corresponds to the letter “T” – with an equally weird text-to-speech mentioning “her”). The second one, meanwhile, appears on the final title card in “Like Lions” (notable for being the only of the three title cards with an actual date, rather than something vague like “2 months later, October”), which is the event where Himawari’s paradise gets derailed twice: first by the sudden call from Ami, and then by “real” Himawari herself.
So what is the significance of these dates? Well, considering that two – or potentially three, if that claim that I cannot find the source of is indeed correct – of them seem to be directly related to our happy little sunflower (in fact, the entire sixth Beach event chain is quite unambiguously connected to her, for self-explanatory reasons), I think that it’s exceedingly clear what – or, rather, *who* – should be our main starting point if we want to make an attempt of trying to get to the bottom of this, even if it means accepting the predominantly speculative nature of the whole process.
(Which, unfortunately, also means that I am a fucking liar, because I explicitly promised that that none of the mysteries in this post will in any way involve Himawari. Whoops… Oh well.)
Now, ignoring the year for a second and looking at just the first part of the dates, “December 28th" as the date of birth followed by “January 1st” as the date of death line up pretty neatly with the “death certificate for an infant” interpretation, since the child would have been less than a weak old at that point. The year part, of course, doesn’t make sense, since both dates read “2020”, which following the normal chronological order would necessarily imply that the owner of that death certificate, whoever it is, died almost twelve whole months before Himawari was born, naturally excluding her from the list of potential suspects – except, well, the Wishing Well is a timey-wimey magic bullshit land where it can be any year you want for as long as you want, and so the “same year” discrepancy does not necessarily disprove shit.
Furthermore, there have been at least two Happy Scenes actively featuring newborn Himawari, in one of which Akira is shown to be severely struggling with raising her alone (“Arms Bent Back”), while in the other she is miraculously saved by Ayane from a situation that would otherwise almost certainly lead to her being injured, if not worse (“Sally Sells Seashells”). And that is without bringing up the still-unexplained Unnamed Baby from “Trinity Pt. III: Non Est Deus” (who, just to remind everyone, was canonically stillborn), or the reality of Ayane unwillingly getting the quickest abortion in Kumon-mi thanks to the Reset shenanigans – and, obviously, there is *no chance in hell* that the exact sixteen-year difference between the date of death on the certificate and Aomori-Himawari’s metaphorical “death” is *just* a happy coincidence. Point is, provided that even a few of these narrative connections are actually correct and not just a product of my overly active imagination, there appears to be a decently strong thematic implication of Himawari either experiencing a very difficult early childhood or suffering some unfortunate (and likely lethal) complication during birth/in her infancy.
And if I *really* wanted to go full schizo, then I could *also* cite that one relatively obscure “current Ami is the result of a wish made by Sekai” theory that dates back to somewhere around 0.45 (with the wish itself in this case being to drastically alter the course of events and allow Ami – the child Sekai was already physically pregnant with at the time – to be born safely, rather than dying in the womb like she was originally supposed to) and directly apply it to Ayane without even really having to change anything:

Thus, the Himawari we know instead comes from *that* secondary reality: a reality where she was born healthy and lived a relatively normal, happy life together with her parents – which importantly doesn’t contradict Himawari’s own claim that she is “[Akira’s] real, blood-related future daughter” from “Aomori”, because the exact mechanics at play here are notably different between the specifics of how Maya came into existence (and this Hima wouldn’t know shit about what happened in the so-called “original” world anyway).
